item.title: Exercising as We Age
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham (March 11, 2026)

When you hit 50, you may still approach physical activity based on your experiences in your thirties or forties. Theresa MacPhail, a contributor to The Guardian, asked if the anti-aging messaging has resulted in a new problem of injuries from over-exercising. Weill Cornell Medicine geriatrician Dr. Emily Finkelstein advises us to change our expectations and how we exercise as we age.

Changes in the Body with Aging

  • The peak for muscle mass and performance is in our mid-thirties, according to Dr. Emily Finkelstein. She says that we need to “be flexible in terms of what we’re doing and expecting of ourselves.” Sarcopenia, or age-related loss of muscle mass, affects balance and strength. Starting in your 30s, you lose about 3-8 percent of your muscle mass per decade, and more after turning 60.
  • Johns Hopkins Medicine notes that older bodies are more likely to have stiff tendons, decreased strength, and reduced range of motion, which all contribute to injuries such as back strain, sprains, and muscle and tendon injuries.
  • Balance, coordination, and proprioception decline, increasing fall risk.
  • Cardiovascular capacity — the heart and lungs’ ability to take in oxygen and convert it into energy (VO2 max) — decreases.
  • Recovery takes longer.
  • Decrease in bone density (osteopenia/osteoporosis) for postmenopausal women (lower estrogen). For men, testosterone levels continue to decline, reducing muscle mass and energy levels.
  • Knee issues, such as cartilage or ligament tears. Women are more vulnerable because of wider hips, which create greater stress on the knee during physical activity.

What You Can Do

The Heart Research Institute’s main message is to “keep moving throughout your life. Sustained exercise is what benefits health most.” For those in their sixties, Rachel Straub, MS, CSCS, co-author of Weight Training Without Injury, comments that the sixties “are the most important time in your life to exercise.” She emphasizes the need to be consistent and use proper form.

Dr. Melissa Leber, associate professor of orthopedics and emergency medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine, has a formula:

  • In your fifties: spend 50 percent of total exercise time on strength training and 50 percent doing cardio.
  • In your sixties: do 60 percent strength and 40 percent cardio.
  • In your seventies: 30 percent of a workout should be cardio.

Types of Exercise in Your Fifties and Beyond

The Australian Institute of Fitness suggests the following appropriate exercise types, focusing on mobility, longevity, and quality of life:

  • Strength and balance training, including resistance bands, light dumbbells, and bodyweight exercises (doing pushups, squats, lunges, and crunches). When performing strength exercises, quality is essential, so be mindful of the control and precision of your movements. Strength training prevents falls and improves balance. Strong muscles support bones and protect joints. An additional benefit of strength training is its impact on brain health. A study in England found that middle-aged women with stronger legs showed slower cognitive aging, with their brains aging structurally and functionally better. If you fall, you will fall differently, and your recovery time will be shorter. As Alexis Coslick, DO, a sports medicine and rehabilitation expert at Johns Hopkins Howard County Medical Center, states, “Regular strength exercise can actually prevent you from becoming disabled.” Another benefit is that strength training helps improve digestion and reduces your risk of chronic health problems such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease. To build your balance, Coslick suggests practicing standing on one leg with your eyes closed (have something nearby to support you if you lose balance). To make sure you do this daily, try brushing your teeth while standing on one leg.
  • Water aerobics provides resistance without stressing joints.
  • Tai chi and chair yoga increase flexibility, coordination, and fall prevention. These types of fitness are excellent for balance and relaxation. Dr. Peter Wayne, research director of the Osher Center for Integrative Medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, comments that tai chi is roughly, depending on intensity, at the same level as a brisk walk, and some research suggests it is also similar to more vigorous forms of weight training.
  • Walking clubs or dance classes provide opportunities for socialization and cardiovascular health that are low-impact. Walk fast enough so your breathing rate increases, but you are still able to talk (moderate intensity) and you “break a sweat.” If you have been a runner, walking is less impact and can be as effective as running for reducing the risk of chronic conditions.

Tips When Exercising as an Older Adult

  • Include longer warm-ups and cool-downs, and allow modifications.
  • Avoid isolation by participating in group fitness.
  • Avoid high-risk activities that increase the risk of falls and injury (high-impact activities or complex agility drills).
  • Have a realistic and adaptive mindset.
  • Go for variety — Sarah Witkowski, an exercise physiologist and associate professor at Smith College, tells The New York Times that to maximize benefits, you want to “keep your body guessing.” Variety is also good for heart health, including blood pressure. Small changes are beneficial. An example is lunging in different directions or doing lunges with overhead dumbbell presses, or changing your walking routine by choosing a route with more hills or walking as fast as you can.
  • Make your exercise plan progressive. Physiotherapist Lauren Lynass of the fitness platform [P]rehab advises people to continually increase the weight they lift or the number of repetitions.
  • Reduce stress on joints — for example, do a warm-up, wear the right kinds of shoes, and maintain a healthy weight to lessen stress on the knees. Consider exercising in water, which provides buoyancy and reduces joint stress.
  • Don’t push through pain — consult your doctor or a physiotherapist to guide you on appropriate exercises, especially if you have chronic conditions. With aging, chronic conditions increase. Move as your level of physical fitness allows, with the goal of moving more and sitting less.
  • Be aware that recovery takes longer for older adults — use gentle stretching daily, prioritize sleep, hydrate frequently, and avoid alcohol (alcohol impairs muscle repair). According to the Australian Institute of Fitness, recovery days still include activity, such as light walking or mobility work. How do you know if you have done too much exercise? It is normal to have a little muscle soreness after workouts, especially in the beginning. If you are not recovering between workouts, you could be overdoing it and need to reduce the intensity or frequency of your workouts until you find the “sweet spot.” You want to do an exercise routine you enjoy to maintain it.
  • Have a backup plan if you injure yourself — for example, adjust your routine. For example, Dr. Leber suggests that if you sustain an injury while running, replace running with a modified strength-training routine and a lower-impact activity, such as swimming. When you return to running, run less frequently and shorter distances. To avoid injury or overuse, take one to two days off for rest.

Consult Your Doctor

Speak with your doctor before commencing exercise — especially if you have a chronic health condition such as diabetes, high blood pressure, heart or lung disease, osteoporosis, a neurological disease, or mobility issues such as arthritis or poor balance. Harvard Medical School reports that people who have been inactive but start doing regular, moderate-intensity exercise reap the most benefit.

Important — it is essential to determine the physical activities you enjoy and can maintain regularly.

Resources

  • SAFE website — developed by the Geriatric Division of Medicine at the McGill University Health Centre (MUHC), SAFE is a series of exercise videos with one goal: to improve your quality of life. The prevention of falls, as well as overcoming the fear of falling, is a big part of that. SAFE will help make you feel stronger and more confident. You can click on the video (found on the right side of the homepage) featuring Dr. José A. Morais, Director, Division of Geriatric Medicine, to learn more about SAFE.
  • Choose to Move Program website — a free and flexible program that provides you with the motivation and support to become more active. It can help you integrate activity into your daily routine, meet new friends, and make a positive change. It is for anyone aged 55 and older who wants to become active, regardless of ability. If you live in BC, you can join them either in person or become part of their thriving online Choose to Move community.
  • Active Aging Canada website — features a physical activity directory. Older adults often don’t know how to become physically active, or how to keep doing so safely. This physical activity directory helps connect you to active aging resources to help you get and stay physically active.
  • Canada’s 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for 65 plus website and 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for 18 to 64 website
  • US MedlinePlus Exercise for Older Adults website

item.title: Physical Activity for the Older Adult
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, Group Fitness Instructor (May 2024)

According to Canadian government guidelines, “Children and youth should get at least 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous physical activity involving a variety of aerobic activities. Adults, including seniors, should accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity per week.”

“On the bright side of this issue, decades of research has made clear that the changes in physical and mental capacities that occur with aging, the rate at which those changes occur, and the extent to which they occur can all be positively modified by a healthy lifestyle that includes regular physical activity and a nutritious diet. Equally positive is that regular physical activity improves a variety of health outcomes that are particularly relevant to older adults.”1

What Changes with Aging?

A variety of changes occur in the body during aging. Simple tasks such as opening jars, lifting groceries, walking up or down stairs, rising easily from a chair, and maintaining balance can become much more difficult as one ages. As well, body weight tends to increase in many people after age 25. After age 65, body weight tends to gradually decrease in many older adults as appetite and physical activity decline and muscle mass is lost at an accelerated rate.

Although some changes are unavoidable, most of us can see positive results by eating a nutritious diet and participating in regular physical activity.

Here is a list of some of the basic changes which occur as we age2:

  • Height decreases starting around age 35 due to compression of the gelatinous discs between vertebrae.
  • Strength and neuromuscular function deteriorate, which can eventually interfere with daily activities.
  • Some types of muscle fibres are lost.
  • Muscle mass can begin to decline as early as age 30.
  • An increase in body fat can occur.
  • Maximal heart rate decreases with age at a rate of 1 beat per minute per year.
  • Maximal stroke volume declines slightly with age, which is due to increased stiffness of the left ventricle and large arteries.
  • Bone mineral content falls as bone synthesis slows and bone resorption increases.
  • Reflexes slow and motor unit activation falls.

Most of these changes can be slowed or even improved with regular physical activity.

Health Benefits of Regular Physical Activity for Older Adults3

  • Improved ability to accomplish activities of daily living
  • Improved sleep quality, functioning and feelings of well-being, as well as perceived quality of life
  • Increased loss of fat weight and increased prevention or minimization of weight gain
  • Reduced risk of falls and related injuries
  • Increased prevention or remediation of frailty and sarcopenia (see definition below)
  • Reduced risk of cardiovascular diseases and osteoarthritis
  • Improved physical function in multiple sclerosis
  • Improved memory, processing speed, attention, and executive function (task initiation, emotional control)
  • Reduced symptoms of depression, anxiety, and dementia
  • Reduced risk of breast, colon, bladder, endometrial, esophageal, kidney, lung, and stomach cancers
  • Reduced risk of (and part of treatment for) diabetes and hypertension
  • Improved physical function in Parkinson’s disease and spinal cord injury

A Healthy Diet Is as Important as Exercise

“Older adults should strive to consume diets that are sufficient in energy (calories), protein, vitamins D and B12, omega-3 fatty acids, and antioxidants provided by whole foods (fruits and vegetables). A nutritious diet and regular physical activity help preserve muscle mass and neuromuscular4 function with aging.”5

“In addition to helping support muscle strength and mass in older adults, diets higher in protein (e.g. 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight per day) is associated with greater weight loss, more fat loss, and better protection of lean body mass.”6

“After retirement, many older adults move to warmer climates where staying well hydrated can be challenging. Being even slightly dehydrated day after day can impair cognitive function and increase the risk of chronic kidney disease.”7

“The muscle cells of older adults become less sensitive to the amino acids supplied by the diet (anabolic resistance), so muscle protein synthesis tends to be lower compared to younger adults. For this reason, adults should try to consume 40 grams of high-quality protein8 after exercise to optimize muscle protein synthesis.”9

How Can Exercise Training Benefit Older Adults?

“After age 60, the failure rate for opening the lid on a jar rises substantially. Loss of strength and muscle mass are due to [many things, including] … reduced physical activity, and inadequate protein intake.”10

“After age 40, sedentary individuals lose an average of 1% of their muscle mass each year along with a loss in strength that averages 3% per year. The severe loss of muscle mass and functional strength associated with aging and a sedentary lifestyle is called sarcopenia, a word coined in 1988 that means ‘poverty of flesh’ in Greek. Sarcopenia occurs as a result of poor diet and a lack of exercise, leading to a gradual decline in muscle mass and strength.”11

“Strength training can slow the loss of certain types of muscle fibres, and physical activity that incorporates weight-bearing exercises helps slow bone loss. Reducing the loss of muscular strength, muscle mass, and bone mass during aging is critical in maintaining the ability to live independently, decreasing the incidence of accidental falls, promoting more rapid recovery from injury and illness, and improving the overall quality of life.

“With age, the normal close relationship between muscle mass and muscle strength is altered. Many older adults lose substantial muscle mass as they age, but if properly trained, can maintain sufficient muscle strength to preserve functional capacity and independence. It is also important that older adults maintain muscle endurance because leg muscles that fatigue quickly increase the risk of falling.

“Proper strength training improves an older adult’s ability to voluntarily recruit and activate the appropriate muscles. As well, improvements in muscle strength, endurance and power in older adults prolongs the ability to live independently, to accomplish activities of daily living, to recover more quickly from illness and injury, and to reduce the risk of falling.

“Endurance training has little impact on the loss of muscle mass with age. Only strength training preserves muscle mass with age while endurance training can slow the decline in breathing and respiration rates. Being physically fit also lowers the risk of heart attack and improves the outcome when a heart attack does occur.”12

“Regular physical activity lowers the risks associated with heat and cold exposure. Heat stress in particular can be a problem for older adults, especially for those who are ill or at a very low level of fitness. When older adults are exposed to heat stress, blood flow to the skin and sweating are less than in younger adults, causing core temperature to rise more quickly. Fortunately, aerobic training can improve blood flow to the skin, increase sweating, and enhance the distribution of blood flow among skin, active muscles, and internal organs. These adaptations improve heat tolerance in older adults.

“With cold exposure, the blood vessels of the skin constrict less in older adults; because muscle mass is typically lower, older adults have a reduced ability to generate and retain metabolic heat. These changes make older adults (especially the elderly) more susceptible to the cold.”13

Low bone mineral density in swimmers and cyclists appears to be due to increased bone resorption (minerals move from bone into the blood) during training along with a lack of adequate stress and strain to stimulate bone formation. Weight-bearing activities are better for bone health because bones are exposed to more stress and strain, stimulating bone-building osteocyte activity.14

Considerations in Designing Training Programs for Older Adults

Here are a few suggestions15:

  • Include all aspects of physical fitness, including basic aerobic conditioning as well as conditioning exercises to improve muscular strength and mass.
  • Multicomponent activities help improve agility, balance, and coordination.
  • Intensity is more important than duration at improving physical function and health outcomes.
  • Body-weight exercises (squats, lunges, toe stands, knee curls, pelvic tilts, and back extensions) can improve functional capacity and muscular strength.
  • Strength training can also improve the aerobic capacity of older adults, particularly those who do little aerobic exercise.

Summary16

  1. In sedentary individuals after age 40, the decline in aerobic capacity and muscular function (muscle mass, strength, etc.) approximates 1% to 2% each year.
  2. The gradual reduction in aerobic capacity is largely a result of lack of exercise.
  3. Loss of muscular function with aging is due to many things, including inadequate dietary protein intake and reduced physical activity.
  4. With proper training, older adults can improve all aspects of physical fitness, although not to the levels achievable when they were younger.
  5. Sarcopenia among the elderly increases morbidity and mortality but can be reversed with proper diet and exercise.
  6. For older adults who are not able to meet current physical activity guidelines for exercise, small and brief bouts of activity such as stair climbing or brisk walking done on a regular basis (e.g. 3 days per week) can also confer benefits to fitness and health.
  7. Physical activities that engage many muscle groups and require whole-body movements improve overall fitness and significantly reduce the risk of falling.

item.title: Exercise and Viruses: Exercise Immunology
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham

This article could be about whether or not you should exercise when you have a virus.

Could. That’s the important word in that sentence.
Because that is not what this article is about.

Instead, this article is about whether or not the exercise you have done in the past will help you fight viruses on any particular day — today, tomorrow, or in the future. In other words, does exercise strengthen your immune system? Will exercise help you to do battle with a virus?

Exercise Immunology

There is a fairly strong body of evidence that exercise will indeed help your immune system.

Dr. David C. Nieman, from Appalachian State University, published in 20031 the results of his research in a document titled “Current Perspective on Exercise Immunology.” His introduction states:

By far, the most important finding that has emerged from exercise immunology studies is that positive immune changes take place during each bout of moderate physical activity. Over time, this translates to fewer days of sickness with the common cold and other upper respiratory tract infections. This is consistent with public health guidelines urging individuals to engage in near-daily physical activity of 30 minutes or more. [My emphasis.]

It should be noted, however, that Dr. Nieman says there is a tipping point where activity is less helpful, especially when other factors are involved:

Risk of upper respiratory tract infections can increase when athletes push beyond normal limits. The infection risk is amplified when other factors related to immune function are present, including exposure to novel pathogens during travel, lack of sleep, severe mental stress, malnutrition, or weight loss. Many components of the immune system exhibit adverse change after prolonged, heavy exertion lasting longer than 90 minutes. These immune changes occur in several compartments of the immune system and body (eg, the skin, upper respiratory tract mucosal tissue, lung, blood, and muscle). During this “open window” of impaired immunity (between 3 and 72 hours, depending on the immune measure), viruses and bacteria may gain a foothold, increasing the risk of subclinical and clinical infection. [My emphasis.]

His final conclusion is:

In general, if symptoms are from the neck up, moderate exercise is probably acceptable (and some researchers would argue even beneficial) when an athlete is sick, whereas bed rest and a gradual progression to normal training are recommended when the illness is systemic.

So, in the end, this article does include one small bit of advice about whether you should exercise while you have a virus. But here’s the more important message to get from what has been said so far: Since heavy exertion may weaken the immune system, it is important to concentrate on moderate activity on a daily basis.

Moderate Activity

What does “moderate activity” mean? It is different for every person, depending on your age, gender, and general health.

In most studies, people who walk 35-45 minutes a day fare better than those who don’t exercise at all, with “about 50% fewer days with cold symptoms.”

Studies vary, of course, as to what it means to exercise moderately. In the fitness industry, moderate exercise is achieving a heart rate that is within 50 to 60 percent of your maximum heart rate. (See below for how to calculate this.) But what “moderate activity” is will be different for each individual.

Here are some suggested activities for a normal adult with no health issues:

  • Walking two miles in 30 minutes
  • Biking five miles in 30 minutes
  • Swimming laps for 20 minutes
  • Running one and a half miles in 15 minutes
  • Doing water aerobics for 30 minutes
  • Playing volleyball for 45 minutes
  • Playing pick-up basketball for 20 minutes
  • Jumping rope for 15 minutes
  • Walking stairs for 15 minutes
  • Dancing for 30 minutes

Other daily activities which also qualify as moderate activity:

  • Washing your car for 45 minutes
  • Gardening for 45 minutes
  • Raking leaves for 30 minutes
  • Vacuuming for 30 minutes

To be absolutely certain that you are reaching the right heart rate level, you can learn to count your heartbeats.

Here is how it’s done: Subtract your age from 220. That is your maximum heart rate. Then calculate 50% and 85% of that number because you do not want to exercise at your maximum heart rate. You will end up with two numbers that give a target range for your heart rate while exercising.

Example: A 70-year-old woman would subtract 70 from 220 to get a maximum heart rate of 150 (220 − 70 = 150). However, she does not want to exercise with her heart beating at 150 beats per minute. Instead, she should exercise at 50-85% of her maximum heart rate, which would be between 75 and 128 (150 × 0.50 = 75 and 150 × 0.85 = 128). Every time she checks her heart rate while exercising, it should be between those two numbers.

Why Does Moderate Activity Help the Immune System?

Research has shown that “during moderate exercise, several positive changes occur in the immune system.” Moderate activity does not release or elevate stress hormones or pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines. Stress hormones, if activated, can suppress immunity. Cytokines are indicative of intense metabolic activity.

Although the immune system returns to pre-exercise levels very quickly after exercise, each session represents a boost in immune surveillance that appears to reduce the risk of infection over the long term.

Conclusion

One can conclude from the research that moderate activity is good for humans in almost any situation, and it can actually enhance the immune system, making you less likely to have trouble fighting off a virus.

Oscar Wilde said, “Everything in moderation, including moderation.” It applies in exercise as well as in every other aspect of our lives. High-intensity exercise may be worthwhile at times, but moderation in our daily activities is worth considering.

item.title: Menopause and the Merits of Physical Activity
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified Fitness Instructor

The headline to the article reads, “Restoring Trust in Menopause Management: Menopause hormone therapy is not a panacea, and physical activity remains a critical intervention.” Dr. Louise Tulloh, a sports medicine doctor at North Sydney Orthopaedic and Sports Medicine Centre in New South Wales, Australia, wrote the article.

This June 2025 British Journal of Sports Medicine article by Louise Tulloh begins with this comment: “This editorial highlights the effects of menopause on the musculoskeletal system and the critical role physical activity can play in fostering musculoskeletal health and well-being during and after menopause.”

After discussing the more traditional treatments for menopause, including (of course) hormone replacement therapy, the article has a section titled “Physical Activity as Medicine.”

“Beyond symptom control, menopause significantly alters long-term health trajectories.” There are increased cardiovascular and cardiometabolic risk factors once menopause occurs, including hypertension and insulin resistance. Bone loss accelerates, increasing fracture risk, and dementia becomes more common.

Given these broad systemic effects, physical activity emerges as a critical, non-pharmacological intervention with multi-system benefits:

  • Bone health: Resistance and impact training enhance or preserve Bone Mineral Density (BMD) in postmenopausal women, even those with osteopenia or osteoporosis. Balance training can reduce falls risk.
  • Muscle strength and health: Progressive resistance training mitigates sarcopenia (loss of muscle tissue as a part of aging) and improves functional outcomes far beyond what pharmacologic interventions can achieve.
  • Metabolic and cognitive health: Exercise improves lipid profiles and insulin sensitivity and has potential neuroprotective effects.
  • Psychological well-being: Physical activity alleviates mood disturbances and sleep dysfunction and helps manage midlife weight gain.

The article goes on to say that “Exercise prescriptions for midlife women should be targeted, progressive and sustainable. While general cardiovascular recommendations remain relevant, emphasis could shift towards high-load resistance training complemented by flexibility and balance work. Clinicians must also be aware of potential barriers: injury risk, such as tendinopathy, may rise during midlife; intense aerobic activity can transiently worsen vasomotor symptoms and the traditional emphasis on ‘cardio for weight loss’ should be rebalanced towards strength training for musculoskeletal health and metabolic benefits.”

“Menopause,” the author states, “represents a critical ‘window of opportunity’ for risk modification. Routine screening for cardiovascular risk factors, bone density and cognitive health should become standard practice for women in their 40s and early 50s. Health professionals must actively dispel myths, communicate realistic expectations for interventions like MHT (Menopausal Hormone Therapy) and promote evidence-based lifestyle strategies such as physical activity.”

The article sums up with these two paragraphs:

Menopause is not merely a biological milestone but a critical turning point for women’s long-term health. As sport and exercise medicine clinicians, our role extends beyond symptom management to advocacy, correcting misinformation, rebuilding trust, setting realistic treatment expectations and promoting strategies such as resistance training and risk factor modification while respecting the intersection between hormonal change and ageing.

We should take the opportunity during midlife health assessment to include exercise counselling that evaluates resistance training and re-evaluates outdated cardio-only-focused paradigms.

item.title: Exercise and Lifespan
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham (April 23, 2025)

Researchers have been investigating strategies to increase the lifespan. Evidence suggests that following a healthy lifestyle, e.g., eating a nutritious diet, not smoking, and exercising regularly, may help extend the lifespan. Finnish researchers from the University of Jyväskylä were interested in examining whether higher levels of physical activity could further increase lifespan, as study author Elina Sillanpää, PhD, stated that “the association between physical activity and lifespan is not as straightforward as commonly thought, which piqued our interest in this topic.” The study aimed to examine the relationship between long-term physical activity and mortality, whether physical activity can counteract genetic risks for disease, and the link between physical activity and later biological aging.

The study involved 22,750 twins in the Finnish Twin Cohort study. Twin studies help researchers to directly test how differences in later life behaviour impact lifespan since twins share similar or identical genetics and early life experiences. Twin studies help to see if a certain trait, illness, or disorder is more impacted by genetics or the environment.

All participants were born before 1958. At three points in time (1975, 1981, and 1990), researchers assessed participants’ physical activity levels and kept track of mortality rates up to 2020. Outcomes evaluated by the researchers included polygenic scoring (to determine inherited disease risk), epigenetic clocks (to estimate biological age), and following twins over time to adjust for genetic confounding (genes that may affect both how active people are and how long they live). The researchers placed participants into one of four groups based on their physical activity data over the 15-year follow-up: sedentary, moderately active, active, and highly active.

The findings, published in the journal European Journal of Epidemiology, included:

  • At the 30-year point, the research team found the most significant difference between the sedentary and moderately active groups. Moderately active individuals had a 7 percent lower mortality risk, and the highly active group did not show additional benefits.
  • Looking at the short and long term, the researchers found a link between more physical activity and lower mortality in the short term. Still, over the long term, highly active individuals had no advantage over those who were sedentary in terms of mortality.
  • Dr. Elina Sillanpää commented that having an underlying pre-disease state can limit physical activity and ultimately lead to death, not the lack of exercise alone. The result is “this can bias the link between physical activity and mortality in the short term.”
  • Additionally, the research team assessed the impact of meeting the recommended physical activity guidelines of 150 to 300 minutes of moderate or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous physical activity weekly (the recommendation by the World Health Organization and the Canadian Society for Exercise Physiology), and how this is related to mortality and genetic disease risk. The research team observed that more intense physical activity did not provide more benefits. Meeting the guidelines did not lower mortality risk or alter genetic disease risk. The study found no statistically significant difference in mortality rates for twins who met the recommendations over 15 years compared to their less active twin pair. Study co-author Laura Joensuu, a postdoctoral researcher, stated, “The widely observed favorable association between physical activity and mortality are based on observational studies that are prone to bias from different sources.” For example, if someone is living with chronic health conditions, they are less active, and it’s natural for individuals close to death to move less, which may cause reverse causality. More physically active people engage in healthier behaviours, such as smoking less and eating healthier. Genetics also partially accounts for how exercise is easy or not.
  • The research team looked at biological aging for a subset of participants. They found a U-shaped relationship, i.e., the least and most active participants experienced accelerated aging. The study press release stated, “Other lifestyles, such as smoking and alcohol consumption, largely explained the favorable associations of physical activity with biological aging.”
  • Study limitations include that the findings applied to Finnish participants, and genetics, the environment, and lifestyle patterns can vary across countries and cultures. The researchers used self-report data for physical activity levels at certain points in time, which is less accurate than continuous monitoring using more objective means of measurement.
  • The bottom line is that physical activity benefits for longevity may not be as straightforward as previously thought.

Does Exercise Intensity Matter?

The study did not find any adverse effects of more vigorous exercise but suggests that moderate physical activity may be as beneficial for longevity.

Study Reviews

  • Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board-certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, shared his thoughts regarding the study with the Medical News Today website. He says that exercise is only one factor that affects longevity. His points include: The findings suggest that exercise’s health benefits “may be confounded by other factors, and that exercise is just one of many behaviors (including eating a balanced diet, avoiding smoking, etc.) that people should try to follow in order to improve their overall health.” Recommendations for exercise are based on several benefits in addition to lifespan, such as improved heart health, reduced risk of depression and anxiety, and reduced stress. He concludes that further research is needed to determine whether these findings apply to other groups beyond the Finnish population followed in this study.
  • Tracy Zaslow, MD, a primary care sports medicine specialist at Cedars-Sinai Orthopaedics in Los Angeles and a team physician for Angel City Football Club and LA Galaxy, commented that this study is just one study, and several other studies show that physical activity increases lifespan. Exercise has several other benefits, including improving quality of life. Muscle mass naturally begins to decline as early as our 30s and 40s. For older adults, strength training addresses the loss of muscle mass and allows them to continue to perform daily activities such as carrying groceries, climbing stairs, or playing with grandchildren. Some people may see the other benefits of exercise as more meaningful than lifespan alone. Researchers are looking more at health span, years spent in good health, as opposed to lifespan or simply extending years lived.
  • George Savva, Senior Research Scientist, Quadram Institute, comments that while some research has shown that people who exercise live longer, other factors explain the association, e.g., genetics, social factors, and health status. He concludes that exercise may play a smaller role in longevity than previously thought. The government should address social and environmental factors that support healthy behaviours such as exercise, since these behaviours are challenging to maintain.

item.title: Exercise and Circulation: Keeping the Blood Moving
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham (© 2024)

The Circulatory System Is Vital to Your Health

The circulatory or cardiovascular system moves blood around the body, carrying food and oxygen to the cells and taking waste away from them. The heart is the centre of this system. This is the route it follows:

Thanks to Cancer Research UK / Wikimedia Commons for the diagram (CC BY-SA 4.0).
  • Blood is pumped from the heart to the lungs where the blood is oxygenated and then returned to the heart.
  • The heart then pumps this oxygen-rich blood around your body through the arteries.
  • Arteries connect to capillaries (the smallest blood vessels), which pass oxygen and nutrients to the cells while removing carbon dioxide and other waste products from the cells.
  • Once there’s nothing left but waste (and very little oxygen), the blood is carried back through veins to the heart.
  • The cycle begins again when the heart pumps the deoxygenated blood back to the lungs to be re-oxygenated.

Because your veins have to overcome gravity, returning blood to your heart from your feet and legs is hard work. The muscles in your lower legs and feet essentially push the blood back up to your heart. As we age, the one-way valves in the veins (which usually prevent blood from falling back down) become weaker and leak, resulting in blood “pooling” in the ankles and feet, causing swelling.


How Can You Increase Circulation?

There are no “magic bullets” for increasing or improving your circulation, but two things will definitely help:

  • Exercise promotes natural movement of blood through the legs and around the body.
  • Healthy eating will reduce your intake of sugar and fat, balance your diet, and increase your dietary fibre. This will allow the blood to flow more easily through the body.

In addition to exercising and eating a healthy diet, you should, whenever possible:

  • Avoid smoking since smoking impairs the circulation of blood; it can cause hardening of the arteries and higher cholesterol.
  • Avoid stress because stress may cause the body to divert blood flow from the feet and the other extremities, causing poor circulation in these areas. Relieving stress through exercise may help to improve blood circulation in the feet.

It is believed that exercise can do the following for your circulatory system:

  • improves the muscles’ ability to pull oxygen out of the blood, reducing the need for the heart to pump more blood to the muscles;
  • reduces stress hormones that can put an extra burden on the heart;
  • slows the heart rate and lowers blood pressure;
  • increases high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and helps control triglycerides;
  • affects the body’s ability to use insulin to control glucose levels;
  • strengthens the heart and lungs.

Why Is It So Important to Get More Oxygen into Our Body?

As we improve our ability to transport and use oxygen, we will have less fatigue for daily activities. This is even more true for those who have an illness or disease where exercise capacity is already lower than for others.

There is evidence that “exercise training improves the capacity of the blood vessels to dilate in response to exercise or hormones, consistent with better vascular wall function and an improved ability to provide oxygen to the muscles during exercise. Studies measuring muscular strength and flexibility before and after exercise programs suggest that there are improvements in bone health and ability to perform daily activities, as well as a lower likelihood of developing back pain and of disability, particularly in older age groups.”

What Exercises Will Help Circulation?

One exercise session is not enough. But the effect of “continued moderate exercise” when combined with other lifestyle modifications can be, according to Dr. Jonathan M. Myers, “dramatic.”

“Many studies documenting the benefits of exercise typically use programs consisting of 30 to 60 minutes of continuous exercise 3 days per week at an intensity corresponding to 60% to 75% of the individual’s heart rate reserve. Most researchers estimate that as much as a 30% to 40% reduction in cardiovascular events is possible….”

From Dr. Myers’ article: “One need not be a marathon runner or an elite athlete to derive significant benefits from physical activity.… the greatest gains in terms of mortality are achieved when an individual goes from being sedentary to becoming moderately active. Studies show that less is gained when an individual goes from being moderately active to very active.”

Here are some suggested activities to help improve and/or maintain your circulatory system:

  • Walking makes the muscles in the legs contract and relax, helps to pump the blood around the body, and lowers blood pressure. It is a low-impact exercise.
  • Swimming has the least impact on the joints. It works the entire body and improves oxygen flow to the heart and lungs. If you swim, you should also be sure that you do weight and balance training separately.
  • Cycling improves circulation in the lower body and can be done outside or in the gym.
  • Dancing is great for improving circulation across the whole body.
  • Heel-toe raises can get the blood pumping again whenever you feel numbness, tingling, or pain in your feet. You can do this sitting or standing, depending on your particular health condition. You can raise heels, then toes, and rock back and forth.
  • Hand exercises can improve poor circulation in the hands, just as heel-toe raises do in the feet. Take each hand and extend the fingers outward so they are spread wide. Then make a fist, hold for a few seconds and stretch fingers outward again. This will keep the hands and fingers from cramping up and allow for better circulation. It is also useful to squeeze a small ball or sponge.
  • Low-impact aerobics can benefit in many ways and is usually combined with strength training and balance training. If possible, attend a class that is intended for older adults.

item.title: Characteristics of a Healthy, Fit Adult
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham (May 29, 2024)

As a fitness instructor of older adults, and being in that category myself at age 78, I am aware of my participants’ various health issues and the daily challenges they face. Most of us who exercise at this age are simply trying to make it through another year in the best health possible. It is quality of life that we hope to maintain. Over time, it becomes more obvious who seems to be the healthiest and fittest and who seems to sabotage their own success...and why.

This is not based on research or a study. These are just my observations after teaching fitness for eighteen years. In no particular order, then, here are the twelve characteristics of a healthy and fit adult which I most commonly see within my regular and persistent fitness class participants.

#1: Has a Routine (and tends to stick to it!)

Everyone benefits from routines. They are particularly helpful when dealing with mental and emotional health, but having a routine for exercise can also be very beneficial. Routines anchor us, give us control over our lives, and reduce stress. When the future is unknown or uncertain, stress will often rear its ugly head. Routines will help to suppress fears of the unknown.

Participants who attend fitness regularly seem to benefit greatly from adhering to a routine. They attend regularly, they learn the routines and exercises, they make friends, and thus class becomes more pleasurable and less stressful. Essentially, they feel a comfortableness with being there and participating.

At the end of the day, they can confidently go to sleep, knowing that they did what needed to be done to remain healthy and fit, rather than berating themselves for not exercising. Those who do not have a routine tend to adapt and adjust on a daily basis, often causing them to miss exercising.

Having a routine allows for a plan for the day which makes most of us feel safer. It gives us calm stability because we know what is happening next. If memory and cognitive issues are beginning to creep in, then having a scheduled routine also makes life easier.

#2: Is Curious

In order to take care of ourselves, both mentally and physically, we have to have a curious mind. We should always ask questions such as:

  • Why does that hurt?
  • What are the side effects of that medication?
  • What does the research say about exercise?
  • How much exercise do I need?
  • What kind of exercise do I need to do?
  • What are the best foods to eat for a healthy body?

Finding answers to questions always makes us less stressed. Curious people make informed decisions about their health because they have asked the difficult questions and sought the best answers they can find. They leave little to chance. (This characteristic also works well in tandem with the fourth characteristic listed below: studies and learns.)

#3: Sees a Doctor When Needed

There are routine medical exams which everyone should be aware of: mammograms, Pap smears, colonoscopies, eye exams, dental checks, or blood tests. We can do some regular check-ups ourselves, such as taking our own blood pressure, but other tests need to be done at the lab, at the doctor’s office, or at the hospital.

Everyone should know when it’s time for a particular test and make the appointment to see their doctor. As we age, there are also vaccines to consider: flu, shingles, and pneumonia, for example.

Those who plan these routine check-ups, and make sure their vaccines are up to date, are more likely to be healthy.

#4: Studies and Learns, and Is a Healthy Skeptic

A healthy adult is also a healthy skeptic. Aware of the scientific method, a healthy adult pays attention to the research and knows when they are being conned. Decisions about health and fitness can often be determined by studying evidence-based research, reading articles from reliable science-based sources, and even taking a course in anatomy or psychology.

A healthy, fit individual is not taken in by alternative medical practices. Each practice is evaluated and the individual determines its merits based on research and personal interactions. When we are desperate for an answer to our health problems, it is fairly easy to be drawn in by con artists. A healthy dose of skepticism will always be a benefit.

#5: Listens to the Advice of Professionals

There are professionals in many fields of health and fitness. It makes sense to listen to experts in the field, whether it is a doctor, a physiotherapist, or a fitness instructor. Healthy, fit older adults know that they can learn much from people who have studied and practiced within their field of expertise, though one should never automatically assume that a person knows what they are talking about.

After seeking advice and recommendations, it is useful to follow up with your own research and studies. If further research reveals nothing questionable, then one can go ahead and follow the advice given. Alternatively, of course, one may decide that the advice was not good and reject it.

#6: Eats a Healthy Diet

While there have been many changes in what constitutes a healthy diet over the years, there have been some things which have remained the same. Applying common sense to your diet will go a long way to improving it. Breaking bad habits is not easy, but one can always benefit from starting some new, better habits.

Generally speaking, we need to reduce our intake of saturated fat, sugar, and salt. Everyone is aware of the value of fruit and vegetables and various sources of protein. Limitation of carbs which come from grains, for instance, can be helpful.

As well, there is a healthy amount of calories one should consume in a day — based on a person’s height and weight. Each person should do their own research to determine how many calories their body requires in a day — and how many calories they can burn in a day.

One does not have to be a nutritionist to pay attention to what one eats. However, it is necessary to educate oneself (refer back to #2 and #4) and find out what works for you. And perhaps most importantly when it comes to diets: avoid fads (see #9 ahead).

#7: Has a Positive, Balanced Outlook

Life has its ups and downs; it is sometimes difficult to find balance. It is perhaps more difficult to maintain a positive outlook on life than it is to do anything else — particularly as we age, face more and more medical challenges, and begin to lose partners, friends, and family members. But we know that having a positive outlook on life will help us get through each day with a little less stress than we might have.

Having a positive outlook also reminds us of the first point on this list: having a routine. Routines help us to focus and stay on target with our goals.

#8: Exercises Correctly, Regularly, and Consistently

If I were listing these in order of importance, this might very well have been #1. People who attend fitness class regularly and consistently are generally healthier and more fit than those who come less often. “But what if they do other things on the other days?” you may ask. Successful exercisers know how much time they need to spend on each type, and by attending regularly they learn the proper forms for strength training and balance exercises. Most people find it easiest to do this in a fitness class or with a personal trainer rather than on their own.

Attending fitness classes regularly allows a participant to learn the steps, hear the instructions about form, and learn about the purposes of each section of the class. The instructor knows how to lead the class through warm-up and cardiovascular exercises, through strength and balance training and flexibility stretches. During the class, the instructor may often give the class helpful and useful information.

It is not rare for a participant to inform me that they injured themselves while doing another activity or sport. This is often because they were trying something too difficult or didn’t properly train or warm up prior to an activity. It is critical, particularly for older adults, that exercise is the right kind for them and repeated often. As well, older adults who have participated in a regular sport for many years may develop repetitive injuries as they age.

#9: Avoids Fads

The fitness industry, like many other areas of our society, is subject to fads and gimmicks. We are often told in commercials to just try “this one simple trick” and you will lose pounds off your waist. Or just “avoid this one food” and you will be sure to lose 50 pounds. These fads come and go. Everyone needs to be cautious of them.

During the 1980s, the main slogan in the fitness industry was “No pain, no gain.” We know now that that was wrong. Smart participants know the difference between evidence-based research regarding fitness — and con men who “sell” you something that will bring you “instant success” without any work at all!

#10: Doesn’t Smoke … and Drinks Responsibly, If at All

Despite years of information regarding the dangers of smoking, there are still many people who smoke. We know that it harms the person who is smoking and we know that second-hand smoke can be equally as harmful. If you are a smoker, the first thing you should do to get more healthy is to try to quit smoking. It is not easy. It is an addiction. But quitting is a good idea.

The damage to our bodies from alcohol is less obvious, perhaps, but still alarming. A smart participant knows that alcohol consumption must and should be limited.

#11: Gets Enough Sleep

Easier said than done. And many older adults have trouble sleeping.

But sleeping is vital to our good health. We cannot possibly survive without sleep. Much research about the importance of sleep has come out in the last couple of decades. We know that we can literally get sick from lack of sleep.

If you have a serious insomnia problem, you need to seek assistance and guidance. If you have problems with sleeping, you should see your doctor or even ask to attend a sleep clinic. Finding answers to your insomnia is essential for good health.

#12: Gets Dental and Eye Care

For some strange reason, in our society we have separated dental care from the rest of our health care issues. But having strong teeth and gums is essential for our well-being. Pain and discomfort wear a person down. Everyone should see a dentist at least once a year — more if you have unique problems. Daily care at home, of course, includes routine brushing and flossing.

Those of us who wear glasses know how important vision is. We can’t and don’t take it for granted. As we age, there are more conditions that can be harmful to our eyes — cataracts and glaucoma being two of the most common. Regular check-ups become as important as going to the dentist once a year. If you have any difficulty with your vision, you should have your eyes checked as soon as possible.

Conclusion

None of these characteristics comes easily and without effort, but they can and should be cultivated by anyone who wants to be healthier and fitter. A certain amount of determination is required to set new goals for yourself and then live up to them.

I am a BCRPA-certified fitness instructor in Vancouver, BC. I teach four classes at the West End Community Centre in Vancouver, BC, mostly designed for the older adult. The Inevitable Disclaimer: Everything published here expresses only my opinion, based on my training and research. What you do with the information is entirely your own responsibility. I am not liable for any injury you suffer that seems to be related to anything you read here. Always consult your doctor before beginning an exercise program.

item.title: Breathing & Relaxation Are Important to Our Health
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

We do it every day, seven days a week: We breathe. We rarely even think about it, yet, like every other part of our body, our lungs require care as well as exercise.

While breathing in, we take in oxygen; while breathing out, we eliminate carbon dioxide and water. With the help of the heart, this process — a complex one which will not be described here — delivers oxygen to the body. Many people don’t realize that the build-up of carbon dioxide — even more than the lack of oxygen — is what causes us to take a breath.

Responding to our body’s needs at any given moment, the brain regulates the rate and depth of breathing so that the right amount of oxygen is delivered to the muscles and organs. During rest, carbon dioxide levels — and therefore breathing rates — are lower. By contrast, carbon dioxide levels in the blood increase during exercise, and so breathing rates go up.

Breathing rates vary from person to person. The average respiratory rate reported in a healthy adult at rest is usually given as 12 breaths per minute. Sometimes, at the end of fitness class, I ask you to listen to your breathing. Chances are, it’s a bit higher right after exercise and will slow down as you relax.

According to Wikipedia, average respiratory rates per minute by age are:

  • Newborns: 44 breaths
  • Infants: 20–40 breaths
  • Preschool children: 20–30 breaths
  • Older children: 16–25 breaths
  • Adults: 12–20 breaths
  • Adults during strenuous exercise: 35–45 breaths
  • Athletes’ peak: 60–70 breaths

The aging process may reduce oxygen blood levels by as much as 20%. Without good breathing, stale air gets stuck in the tissues of the lungs and prevents fresh oxygen from reaching the bloodstream. Side effects of poor breathing can include overall fatigue, mental “fuzziness”, poor posture, sore rib cage and/or sore muscles.

Within limits, breathing can be controlled consciously, but most of the time the system works on its own. Conscious control of breathing occurs in meditation or during exercise, or in speech or vocal training.

★ ★ ★

Here are four suggestions to keep your lungs strong:

  1. Stop smoking: Get help through your doctor or a stop-smoking program.
  2. Get your annual flu shot: It will protect you from developing potentially deadly complications from respiratory infections.
  3. Exercise: This improves lung capacity and gets more oxygen to your brain.
  4. Eat right and drink plenty of fluids: Proper nutrition and hydration are important, not only for the lungs, but for all of our body’s systems.
★ ★ ★

Breathing exercises can help keep the lungs fit. We do some of these exercises in both Light Fit and Adapted Fit, and you can find many others on the internet.

When we are anxious or tense, we tend to breathe shallow and high. Abdominal breathing — which means to breathe fully from the bottom of your lungs — is considered one of the best breathing exercises of all. It is good for relaxation, release of tension, and anxiety control.

Breathing in (left) and breathing out (right). Thanks to OpenStax, Anatomy & Physiology, for the image (CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

To practice abdominal breathing, follow these steps:

  • Place both hands on your abdomen.
  • Inhale through your nose slowly and deeply. Imagine the air filling up the bottom of your lungs first and then slowly rising to the top. As your lungs fill up with air, they will push the diaphragm down, which pushes the internal organs to the side, allowing your stomach to rise. You should see your hands rise, but your chest should move only slightly. (Count to 6.)
  • Pause for a moment. (Count to 8.)
  • Exhale through your mouth, pursing your lips to make it come out slowly and evenly. (Count to 12.) Note: It should take twice as long to exhale as to inhale.
  • Repeat the entire process 2-3 times daily.
★ ★ ★

In fitness class, I tell you to BREATHE. Don’t hold your breath at any time during exercise. Technically, there is a right and a wrong way to breathe while weightlifting, but HOW you breathe is LESS important than the simple fact that you BREATHE.

If you wish to have a pattern to your breathing while lifting weights, there is a simple rule to follow: Since it’s harder to lift a weight than it is to lower it, you need to synchronize the breathing with the difficulty of the movement: Inhale when the weight is being lowered and exhale when the weight is being raised.

There are two ways to achieve this: (1) Begin at the beginning of the exercise, inhale, then exhale as you exert yourself with the upward or harder movement, or (2) Move to the top of the exercise, inhale as you come down, and exhale as you push back up. If you find this uncomfortable, don’t worry about it. Remember what has already been said: How you breathe is less important than the simple fact that you breathe.

item.title: Brain Exercises: A Few Ideas
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-Certified Fitness Instructor

We know that if we exercise the brain, we may decrease the chances of getting Alzheimer’s or dementia by encouraging new nerve cell growth and increasing communication between nerve cells. Some studies suggest that these activities will continue to stimulate the brain for up to five years.

Below are some ways you can exercise your brain (in addition to attending fitness class). There are many possibilities; these are just a few. The goal is simple: challenge the brain to do something different. If you already do them, great! If you find something new on the list and it intrigues you, feel free to give it a try.

New Skills

🚶 Physical

  • Try a new physical activity: golf, lawn bowling, swimming, tai chi, dancing, yoga, badminton — to name just a few.
  • Challenge your non-dominant hand or foot: Eat or write with the non-dominant hand; shift your weight to the non-dominant foot while at the kitchen sink.

🃏 Mental

  • Learn to read music and/or play an instrument (if you played an instrument in your youth, play it again).
  • Play card games or purchase apps on your phone to play.
  • Learn a foreign language.
  • Learn to use new technology: computers and accessories, phones, video games.

🧠 Brain Games

  • Do crossword or Sudoku puzzles.
  • Try math problems or brain teasers.
  • Memorize a list worth remembering (e.g. Canadian provinces).
  • Memorize poetry, literary passages, or famous sayings that you enjoy.
  • Don’t look at your shopping list but, before you buy, check it.

📖 Reading and Writing

  • Read out loud (to your spouse, your grandchildren, or your friends).
  • Read magazines, newspapers, novels, non-fiction — whatever you enjoy.
  • Keep a diary of your daily activities.
  • Write your own poetry or prose.

🛌 Healthy Habits

  • Exercise (at least 30 minutes 5 times per week).
  • Build muscles (moderate levels 2-3 times a week).
  • Eat a brain-healthy diet. (Include nuts, whole grains, and fresh produce. Avoid trans fats, but enjoy a glass of red wine and a dark chocolate square occasionally.)
  • Establish a regular sleep schedule. (Note: If you have specific problems with insomnia, you may need to see your doctor.)
  • Do breathing exercises or meditate regularly.
  • Each time you shop, take a different route.

item.title: Balancing & Breathing Exercises You Can Do at Home
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-Certified Fitness Instructor, Specialist in Third Age and Special Populations

Choose from the following for a 10-Minute Balancing Practice Session

  1. Foot Circles: Point your foot forward, to the side, and to the back, then raise the foot slightly over the floor and circle it in one direction 4 times, then do the other direction. Repeat on the other foot.

  2. Heel-to-Toe Stand: Stand with the toe of one foot touching the heel of the other foot. Close eyes. Balance. Repeat with the other foot in front.

  3. Heel-to-Toe Walk: Walk 4-5 steps with a heel-to-toe position. Try doing it while moving the head side to side. Try doing it while your eyes are closed.

  4. Instep-to-Toe Walk: Do the same thing as in the Heel-to-Toe Walk.

  5. Baby Steps Walk: Do the same thing as in the Heel-to-Toe Walk.

  6. Stand on One Leg: Lift one leg as far as a bent knee of 90°. Hold. Repeat on the other leg.


Choose from the following for a 10-Minute Breathing Activity

  1. Abdominal Breathing: Place one hand on chest and the other on abdomen. Breathe in slowly and let abdomen rise. Exhale slowly. Watch abdomen sink.

  2. 4-7-8 Breathing: Inhale for 4 counts. Hold for 7. Exhale for 8.

  3. Bellows Breathing: Breathe in and out; three in one second. Produce quick movement of diaphragm, suggesting bellows. Breathe normally after each cycle. Do not do more than 15 cycles. (Tends to make you dizzy.)

  4. Calm Breathing: Inhale to 5 counts. Hold breath to 5 counts. Exhale to 5 counts. Take 3 normal breaths. Repeat 3 times, or for up to 5 minutes.

  5. Chinese Breath: First short inhale, lift arms straight out in front. Second short inhale, lift arms straight out to sides. Third short inhale, lift arms straight over head. Exhale, arms back down to sides.

  6. Humming Breath: Inhale, fill belly. Fill chest. As you exhale, make a humming sound. Relax.

  7. Progressive Muscle Relaxation: Tense a group of muscles for 7-10 seconds. Release. Go limp. Repeat with another group of muscles.

item.title: Learning Styles
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, Group Fitness Instructor

There are 4 predominant learning styles: Visual, Auditory, Read/Write, and Kinaesthetic. While most of us may have some general idea about how we learn best, often it comes as a surprise when we discover what our predominant learning style is. And we can also have a little of each, depending on what it is we are trying to learn.

Visual Learners

Visual learners learn through seeing, so tools like diagrams, flowcharts, pictures and symbols can be key to understanding new concepts.

As University style lectures tend to neglect visual components, it may be difficult for visual learners to stay focused during a long lecture. When taking notes in class, something to try is developing a system of symbols to replace the written word. For example, instead of writing out “female” each time in your notes, simply use the standard symbol. Or instead of writing that the results of a particular test were positive, insert a smiley face!

For visual learners, it is often far easier for recall to work with images as opposed to working with words, as you will picture the image in your head while recalling it—far more difficult when trying to recall the word itself!

Other tricks to try for visual learners include spatially rearranging your page—instead of writing across a page horizontally, write in a way that is more descriptive of the relationship being described—for example, write the words out in a circular pattern if that more truly represents the relationship you are describing. Also, it can be useful to colour code your notes, to create more visual stimulation.

Visual learners should focus on the following:

  • Use graphs, charts, illustrations, or other visual aids.
  • Include outlines and handouts for the subject matter.
  • Eliminate potential distractions while reading.
  • Use diagrams to help you understand.
  • Leave white space in handouts for note taking.
  • Use illustrations and presentations that use color.

Auditory Learners

Auditory learners learn through listening. As such, attending lectures, tutorials, and group discussions are absolutely essential for these learners (it’s also essential for the rest of us, being a read/write learner is no reason to skip lecture!).

If you’re an auditory learner, focus on text book readings by reading them out loud, so you can hear how the words sound. It can also be really helpful to engage in group discussions about course concepts and topics—create a weekly study group to get together weekly just to talk about the things being discussed in lectures.

Leave lots of extra room on your page when taking notes in lectures, and then return to these notes after you’ve had a chance to discuss the material in further detail—supplement with the new information you have.

Auditory learners should try the following:

  • Begin new material with an understanding of what is coming.
  • Conclude with a summary of what was learned.
  • Try to verbalize the question.
  • Read aloud.

Read/Write Learners

Read/write learners learn through—what else?—reading and writing. As such, university style courses suit these types of learners fairly well—plenty of text books and study notes to read.

If you’re a read/write learner, pay special attention to text book glossaries—better yet, make your own as you progress through a course. After lecture, return to your notes for review, read them over, and then create a new, condensed set of study notes. Lists can also be a very useful tool.

And a good tip for all students is to rewrite explanation and notes out into your own words. If you can’t rewrite a definition or describe a concept in your own words, concisely, there is a good chance that there is an aspect of that concept that you don’t fully understand. Return to this concept for further review.

Kinaesthetic Learners

Kinaesthetic Learners learn through doing. This is perhaps the most challenging learning style for university students, as there are not always many opportunities to engage in hands on learning in lectures. For this reason, labs and tutorials become even more essential for these learners.

While studying, try to incorporate all of your senses into the experience—the more of this you can do, the higher your recall will be, as you’ll have multiple cues.

One way to create more useful study notes if you’re a kinaesthetic learner is to fill your notes with several examples for each concept. Try taking an example from the text, or lecture, or lab, and then try creating your own example. As a general rule, the more personal your created example is, the better your recall will be for that example—and hopefully for the concept it is describing! Also try to make as much use of practise questions and exams as possible.

Kinesthetic Learners should consider these techniques:

  • Use activities that will allow you to move.
  • Play music during activities.

item.title: Health Issues Faced by the Older Adult
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, Group Fitness Instructor

Four health conditions that many older adults often face are:

  1. hearing loss and tinnitus;
  2. cataracts;
  3. depression; and,
  4. dementia.

This article will do a brief review of all four conditions.

Hearing Loss and Tinnitus

These two things — hearing loss and tinnitus — can occur together or separately. Hearing loss — caused by such things as aging or exposure to loud noises — is strongly linked with tinnitus, but some people with hearing loss never develop tinnitus.

Age-related hearing loss is known as presbycusis; it is progressive, occurs in both ears in roughly equal amounts, and affects the high frequencies first. It is the most common cause of hearing loss worldwide and is estimated to affect approximately two-thirds of people aged 70 or older.

The causes of presbycusis are numerous but generally are a result of at least one of four factors:

  1. Continuous exposure to loud noises (such as music or work related noise);
  2. loss of hair cells (sensory receptors in the inner ear);
  3. inherited factors; and,
  4. aging.

There are different types of presbycusis and the type someone has depends on the specific damage that has been done to the inner ear. Two of the most common types are:

  1. Sensory presbycusis: This hearing loss happens when you lose outer hair cells in the organ of Corti at the base of your cochlea.

  2. Neural presbycusis: Your ability to hear relies in part on nerve cells in your cochlea and the auditory pathway to your brain. You lose nerve cells over time as a part of growing older.

Tinnitus (pronounced tih-NITE-us or TIN-uh-tus) is the perception of sound that does not have an external source, so other people cannot hear it.

Tinnitus is commonly described as a ringing sound, but some people hear other types of sounds, such as roaring or buzzing. It is more common than many people realize — surveys estimate that 10% to 25% of adults have it while children can also have it. For children and adults, tinnitus may improve or even go away over time, but in some cases, it worsens with time. When tinnitus lasts for three months or longer, it is considered chronic.

The causes of tinnitus are unclear, but most people who have it have some degree of hearing loss. Tinnitus is only rarely associated with a serious medical problem. However, some people find that it affects their mood and their ability to sleep or concentrate. In severe cases, tinnitus can lead to anxiety or depression.

Currently, there is no cure for tinnitus, but there are ways to reduce symptoms. Common approaches include the use of sound therapy devices (including hearing aids), behavioral therapies, and medications.

Cataracts

A cataract is a cloudy area in the lens of the eye (the clear part of the eye that helps to focus light). They are very common as a person ages. In fact, more than half of all people age 80 or older either have cataracts or have had surgery to get rid of cataracts.

Most cataracts develop when aging or injury changes the tissue that makes up the eye's lens. Proteins and fibres in the lens begin to break down. This causes vision to become hazy or cloudy. Some genetic disorders that cause other health problems can also increase the risk of getting cataracts.

Cataracts can be removed only with surgery. If your cataract symptoms are not bothering you, surgery is not necessary. You should consider surgery when cataracts keep you from doing things you want or need to do.

Depression

Depression is a mood disorder that causes a persistent feeling of sadness and loss of interest. It affects how you feel, think and behave and can lead to a variety of emotional and physical problems.

Why are seniors at risk of depression? Here are some of the reasons:

  1. Loneliness: Many seniors live alone and have limited means to socialize. They often miss the people with whom they once shared experiences and regular conversations — spouses, friends, neighbours, medical providers, and work colleagues. As a result, they are highly susceptible to feelings of loneliness and isolation.

  2. Immobility: Whether because of physical limitations or transportation constraints, or both, many seniors are not as able to do as much or get around as well as they once did. The loss of a driver’s license is particularly frustrating to some older adults, even while others choose to stop driving.

  3. Lack of Independence: As we age, we are naturally less able to do for ourselves. Declining physical health, unstable balance, falls, memory loss, dementia, impaired mobility, frailty — all these factors contribute to a greater reliance on others. Many seniors struggle with their loss of independence and feel helpless and guilty for asking for help from others.

  4. Lack of Purpose: With aging, some things change — retirement, “empty nest”, failing memory — and those changes contribute to a sense of insignificance among the elderly. Add ageism to that and it’s easy to understand why some seniors become despondent.

  5. Fear of the Future: Even the healthiest seniors know that they’ve lived many more years than they have left. The future may bring physical or cognitive decline, financial threats, changing living arrangements, decreased security, death of self or loved ones, and being a burden upon others. These can lead to anxiety and depression.

There are many ways that an older person can fight these aging issues, but the easiest way is to just get involved: volunteer, take a course, go to fitness class, help a friend.

Dementia

Dementia is a term that is used to cover a variety of symptoms associated with declining mental ability. It is a medical condition of the brain and not specifically a psychological or mental illness, although there can be behavioural and psychological symptoms associated with it.

Dementia symptoms are often overlooked because they are simply thought to be signs of normal aging in older adults. However, dementia is not a natural part of aging and its symptoms include:

  • Forgetfulness
  • Memory loss
  • Reduced reasoning
  • Trouble paying attention
  • Impaired judgment and problem solving
  • Visual perception issues that aren’t related to normal age-related changes
  • Changes in personality and behaviour
  • Any other changes that interfere with a person’s normal daily functions

Dementia is a term used to cover symptoms of mental decline, but there are actually many different types of dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease.

While normal aging can affect cognitive and memory performance, dementia—and therefore Alzheimer’s—is not a part of the normal aging process. Here are examples of normal memory loss for older adults:

  • Misplacing car keys every now and then
  • Forgetting very recent events
  • Having trouble finding a word, but then remembering it later
  • Forgetting the name of an acquaintance

These instances are expected as older adults age. However, it’s important to monitor yourself and/or friends or loved ones to see if these issues continue, increase in frequency, or worsen. If they do, you should seek help from a medical professional to determine if they have dementia or Alzheimer’s disease.
