item.title: Aging and Activity
item.description:
What Happens As We Age?

Most of us notice a decline in our body’s ability to move and be active by the age of 30. But, some studies suggest that “participating in regular physical activity can delay the normal aging process by 10 to 20 years.”

Let’s take a look at some of those changes and what types of exercise may help:

  • Cardiovascular and Respiratory Function: Your body’s ability to take in oxygen and transfer it to blood and muscles is known as aerobic capacity; loss of it may tax the heart and lungs, making it harder for you to breathe. Aging and/or disease play a role, but cardiovascular exercise helps maintain aerobic capacity.

  • Muscle Weakness and Loss of Muscle Mass: As our muscles weaken, there are losses in aerobic capacity, bone density, insulin sensitivity, and metabolic rate; it will contribute to increases in body fat, blood pressure, and incidences of cardiovascular disease and diabetes. To counteract the normal loss of muscle mass, older adults will find endurance and resistance training beneficial.

  • Joint Mobility: The ligaments, tendons, muscles, fascia and skin around the joint get stiff and/or shorten as we age, and joint movement can decline 20-50% between 30 and 70. Flexibility can be maintained by safely moving the joints through their full range of motion — but once range of motion is lost, it is difficult to regain.

  • Loss of Bone Mass: Loss of bone mass is a normal part of aging. Fractures are more likely, particularly in the spine, hip and wrist. Studies suggest that exercise helps if it is long-term and involves stressing the skeleton (walking, jogging, stair climbing or squats). For the upper body, resistance training is important.

  • Neurological Function: A lessening of cognitive skills, memory loss, detriments in vision and hearing, loss of motor speed, and balance and gait impairments — all occur as we age. Physical activity has many beneficial effects on memory and cognition, especially if one is challenged to do a variety of tasks at once. There is also evidence that exercise can improve blood supply to the brain, thus stimulating neuronal growth.

Neuroscientists Tell Us What We Can Do

Research reveals that “the best way to forestall or even reverse age-related mental decline is with a regular program of exercise.” They add that “people who exercise regularly can resist this decline.”

Here’s some quotes from the experts:

  1. Dr. Art Kramer, a neuroscientist and director of the Beckman Institute at the University of Illinois, conducted studies that show that even sedentary older adults who begin “regular aerobic exercise programs” can improve cognitive function by 15-20%.

  2. Dr. Brian Christie, another neuroscientist, who teaches at both UBC and UVic, suggests that “the brain is a very demanding organ, requiring vast amounts of nutrients and oxygen.” If we reduce fitness as we age, we “may deprive the brain of the resources it needs to perform well....Exercise [may] actually stimulate growth in the brain.”

  3. Dr. Laura Baker, a neuropsychologist with the Veterans Administration and the University of Washington in Seattle, says there is evidence that “exercise produces growth factors in the brain that preserve and protect neurons.” This may even stimulate stem cells to produce new brain cells — possibly “restoring brain tissue that may have atrophied.”

  4. Dr. Jon Ratey, a psychiatrist at Harvard University, says that this stimulation that Dr. Baker refers to is most likely “because stem cells in the brain are stimulated to produce new neurons....Most studies indicate that forty minutes to an hour of moderately intense aerobic exercise...three or four times a week, will help you reap the cognitive rewards.”

More Research About Aging and Exercise

In the end, we should try to do what's best for ourselves. Here are several studies that tell us more:

  1. A study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine reviewed the histories of 24,281 Canadians. It revealed that “The average yearly healthcare costs for the physically inactive were $1214 higher than healthcare costs of the physically active.”

  2. More than 1500 older adults were involved in a six-year study; the average age was 71 years and 18% of them lived alone. The participants were asked every two years about whether they felt isolated or lacked companionship. People who said they were lonely were more likely to report difficulty in: 1) accomplishing daily living tasks; 2) using their upper body, and 3) climbing stairs. Thirty-eight percent of them reported a decline in mobility, and loneliness was associated with an increased risk of death.

  3. The Longevity Genes Project followed the lives of over 500 Eastern European Jews over the age of 95 along with 700 of their descendants. Responding to many questions, these centenarians exhibited a positive attitude toward life, had an ability to express their emotions, did not display neurotic personalities, and exhibited a high level of conscientiousness. One of the researchers said, “[They] considered laughter as an important part of life and had a large social network. They expressed emotions openly rather than bottling them up.”

  4. A study used data from a survey titled Americans’ Changing Lives, as well as mortality statistics for 1986-2005. It revealed that people who had high levels of social engagement were at a lower risk of death compared to those with less social interaction, even after controlling for other predictors of mortality. Finding ways to interact with others is important: from attending fitness class, to playing bridge, to taking a walk with your grandchild.

  5. Professor Steven N. Blair of the Department of Exercise Science and Epidemiology at the Arnold School of Public Health, University of South Carolina, has been involved in research to determine how much regular physical activity improves our health….at any age. His results were published in an edition of the British Journal of Sports Medicine. Professor Blair says: “There is now overwhelming evidence that regular physical activity has important and wide-ranging health benefits. These range from reduced risk of chronic diseases such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers to enhanced function and preservation of function with age.” As well, “there is strong emerging evidence that activity delays cognitive decline and is good for brain health as well as having extensive benefits for the rest of the body.” Blair discovered that those who exercised lived longer and felt better than those who didn’t. He asserts “that the typical physician is 10-50 times more likely to measure cholesterol, blood pressure, and BMI than to measure fitness.” He recommends that an exercise test be a part of any physical exam.

I teach four classes at the West End Community Centre in Vancouver, BC, mostly designed for the older adult. item.title: Arthritis and Exercise, Part 4: Exercise Guidelines and Considerations
item.description:
Why you Should Exercise if you have Arthritis
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

If you have any form of arthritis, here are some guidelines to follow when exercising:

  1. Expect fatigue: Fatigue is a side effect of the disease, especially with RA. Find a balance between exercise and rest, as you need both.

  2. Expect some pain: You should respect and expect pain, especially during exercise. Modifications need to be made based on your personal pain tolerance.

  3. Use the 2-Hour Pain Rule: If you experience more than typical joint pain two hours after exercise, it indicates that you have overexerted. You need to adjust your workload the next time you exercise.

  4. Respect your limits: Only you know how you feel. If the exercise is uncomfortable or hurts, you should stop, slow down, change weights, rest — whatever seems right for you. Work at your own pace and don’t attempt to keep up with anyone else.

  5. Warm-ups should be long and slow: The warm-up phase is an essential component of the workout. Your instructor should begin with slow, range-of-motion exercises and gentle large muscle movements.

  6. Use heat prior to exercise: A hot shower, heating pad, electric blanket, or hot towel is sometimes recommended before exercise. Heat helps to decrease pain and stiffness and may make exercise easier.

  7. Progress slowly: Modify whenever necessary. Decrease repetitions and speed of the movement when appropriate.

  8. Use proper body mechanics: Use your joints in their most stable position.

  9. Avoid jarring movements: Avoid quick directional changes as they can compromise joints and aggravate joint pain.

  10. Follow the tenets of joint protection: If you follow the basic tenets of joint protection, your joints will be stabilized and in their strongest, most workable position. The basic tenets of joint protection are: (1) do not compromise the joint; (2) limit extreme weight-bearing flexion (e.g. don’t do a deep squat); (3) use positions that stabilize the joint (e.g. keep wrist in line with the arm); (4) never force joints into uncomfortable positions; (5) use stronger joints for support whenever possible; (6) avoid being in one position for a prolonged period of time; (7) conserve energy; (8) avoid overexertion or overloading of joints; (9) use adaptive equipment when necessary; and (10) stop any movement at the point of pain.

  11. Attempt complete and full range of motion movements, as much as can be tolerated: This might be accomplished by decreasing the speed of the movement, a slower tempo of music, warming up with range of motion activities, and flexibility stretching at the end. Some activities reduce or eliminate stress on the joints, such as swimming and gentle walking.

  12. Use isometric exercises: These exercises use a stable joint position. Pressing the hands together, pressing down on a ball, squeezing the ball — these are isometric exercises, and they reduce joint movement yet strengthen muscles.

  13. Increase chest expansion: Do deep-breathing exercises before and after exercise.

  14. Include Relaxation: Relaxation reduces muscular tension and soothes muscles and joints. Every exercise session should end with flexibility and relaxation.

  15. Avoid becoming chilled: Cold drafts and/or becoming chilled while exercising leads to increased muscle tension. Avoid being in front of the fan or near an open window while exercising.

  16. Use appropriate footwear: Find a shoe that provides plenty of room for your toes, a stable and comfortable sole, extra cushioning and space for orthotics, and possibly velcro for easy closure.

  17. Try to exercise at the best time of day for you: People with RA tend to be less stiff and sore later in the day. Those with OA may be better able to tolerate exercise in the morning before activities of the day have increased their pain.

  18. Use medication properly and talk to your doctor: Follow the schedule your doctor has recommended. Let your doctor know how you are feeling and explain what your exercise regimen entails.

These are all things within your control and, if followed, will help you have some control over your condition. Hopefully, your exercise instructor is well-versed in this information, as well, and will help you to exercise properly.

Source: Exercise and Arthritis by Stephanie Harris, MD, and Gwen Hyatt, MS

item.title: Arthritis and Exercise, Part 3: Exercise Design
item.description:
Why you Should Exercise if you have Arthritis
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

We know that regular, moderate physical activity has many benefits. As well, research shows that well-regulated exercise does not produce or aggravate joint symptoms. More specifically, some level of physical activity is necessary to preserve joint function. A combination of aerobic exercise, strength training, stretch and flexibility — taught by a qualified instructor — is the most effective.

The primary goals of an exercise program for those suffering from arthritis are:

  • Restore or maintain joint range of motion: Moving the joints regularly is important to maintain flexibility so that daily activities can be done.

  • Restore or maintain muscle strength: Strengthening exercises can increase tone and functional strength of the muscles surrounding the joint, making it easier to move the joint.

  • Interrupt the Chronic Pain Cycle: When moving the joint is painful, there is a tendency to stop moving it. Continued disuse of the joint may cause stiffness and a shortening of the muscles and connective tissues around the joint (known as joint contracture). Put very simply: loss of movement leads to loss of function.

  • Improve cardiorespiratory endurance: Low-impact aerobic exercise is safe and desirable for individuals with arthritis. Not only does it contribute to one’s overall fitness level, it also will mean less joint stiffness.

  • Improve posture and body awareness: Posture may be improved through balance and coordination exercises.

  • Relieve stiffness: Regular exercise is critical in maintaining ease of movement.

  • Maximize pulmonary function: Breathing and chest expansion exercises encourage maximal lung function.

  • Promote relaxation: Any exercise program requires a relaxation period at the end. Relaxation techniques soothe the muscles and decrease stress.

  • Enhance quality of life: Exercise may improve self-image and self-esteem. Positive social interaction in a class may increase one’s feeling of self-worth and the positive feeling of knowing that you have the ability to take care of yourself.

Source: Exercise and Arthritis by Stephanie Harris, MD, and Gwen Hyatt, MS

item.title: Arthritis and Exercise, Part 2: How to Manage Arthritis
item.description:
Why you Should Exercise if you have Arthritis
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

The most common medications used for arthritis are:

  • analgesics for pain reduction
  • anti-inflammatory agents for inflammation reduction
  • immunosuppressants for immune system suppression
  • antidepressants for helping reduce depression and anxiety

Surgical interventions — to relieve pain and improve function — are becoming more common for RA: hip and knee replacements are the most common, but surgery is also done on shoulders, elbows and ankles.

There are other therapies that seem to help some people — from massage to braces to Chinese medicine. Each person must decide what works for them.

In addition to medical intervention and therapies, there are some simple strategies that can be done by everyone — they can help to control pain, improve independence and quality of life, and slow the progression of the disease.

Here are five strategies that may help:

  • Weight reduction: Even modest weight loss (as little as 5 pounds) may be beneficial by putting less stress on the joints and their function.

  • Rest and relaxation: Deep breathing, visual imagery while listening to music, tensing and relaxing individual muscles, and self-generated meditation exercises — all can be done at the end of an exercise class or alone at home in the comfort of your favourite chair.

  • Joint protection: Limiting stress to the joints is important, so remember these basic principles of joint protection: (1) respect pain; (2) distribute the load over stronger joints; (3) avoid sitting or standing for long periods of time; (4) reduce weight; (5) use good posture and body mechanics; (6) use the minimum amount of force necessary; (7) balance work with rest; and, (8) remain active.

  • Energy conservation: Conserving your energy overlaps with protecting your joints. Planning ahead, organizing tasks, and taking regular breaks will help to conserve your energy.

  • Exercise: See Parts 3 and 4 for exercise guidelines and principles.

Source: Exercise and Arthritis by Stephanie Harris, MD, and Gwen Hyatt, MS

item.title: Arthritis and Exercise, Part 1: Overview of Rheumatic Disease
item.description:
Why you Should Exercise if you have Arthritis
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

Most adults have one or two chronic health conditions by the time they reach 60, but many people manage their disease(s) and live normal and productive lives. Physical disuse and disability in people with chronic disease is, however, a major contributor to premature aging. Dr. Waneen Spirduso in her book, Physical Dimensions of Aging, identifies the three things which contribute to the aging process:

  • Dimension #1: Time. This is the normal aging process, which eventually drains energy and vitality.

  • Dimension #2: Disease. Genetic predispositions to diseases, or exposure to external agents, will damage one or more bodily systems and lead to weakness, fatigue, and frailty.

  • Dimension #3: Disuse. Sitting for long periods of time, extended bed rest, or general inactivity dramatically accelerates aging. “A lifetime of physical disuse can have catastrophic effects on strength, cardiovascular function, mobility, and physical as well as mental function.”

We obviously have little control over the first two dimensions: time and disease. But the third one, disuse, is completely within our control. Arthritis and other rheumatic conditions are among the most common chronic diseases, and they often lead to disuse. What is arthritis? There are two common types:

Osteoarthritis (OA) — the most common form of arthritis which worsens over time — is a progressive joint disease. There is a gradual loss of cartilage from the joints and, for some, joint inflammation. The most common symptoms are pain, stiffness and loss of joint motion. It most often affects the hands, knees, hips, and spine.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune inflammatory disease; the immune system turns against the body, attacking the joints. The lining surfaces of the joints become inflamed; it can also affect the surface surrounding the heart and the lungs. It tends to occur on both sides of the body, usually involving multiple joints of the hands and feet, although any joint can be involved.

There are other types of rheumatic disease but they are not as common as OA and RA. These include: spondyloarthropathy, Reiter’s syndrome, gout, psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, juvenile arthritis, systemic lupus, scleroderma, and fibromyalgia.

The next section will discuss how to manage arthritis.

Source: Exercise and Arthritis by Stephanie Harris, MD, and Gwen Hyatt, MS

item.title: Book 3: Julia
item.description:
Chapter 9: My Childhood

I have always felt that my childhood was almost idyllic. That may seem odd, considering what my mother went through while giving birth to eleven children — one more child than even her own mother had given birth to — as well as the nightmare she lived through with her older sister, Clarinda, and the difficulties with my father.

I was born on 20 October 1861, just a year after my Aunt Clarinda met her death at Sing Sing Prison for Women. My mother had already given birth to six children before me: Samuel, Lafayette, Sarah Etta, Leonard, Susan, and Cassius. Before I arrived, Mother had already lost a son, Lafayette, and a daughter, Susan, and she lost Cassius in December 1862, when I was just a baby. After my birth, she had four more babies — all girls — Bessie, Clarria, Effie, and Flora. Clarria and Flora died as infants, while Bessie and Effie would face much more difficult endings.

I was just four years old when my parents decided that we had to leave West Turin and find a new life in another place. I have little memory of West Turin, though by the time we moved I had been out and about with my older sister, Sarah Etta, many times. For me, Sarah Etta was almost my mother. She once told me that she was given the responsibility of taking care of me almost from the time I was born. She certainly taught me about all that the family had endured before I came along, including a great deal of detail about Aunt Clarinda’s story.

Because of these reminders of what had happened to Aunt Clarinda, I knew from an early age that, even though I was a girl, I had a right to live my life the way I wanted to live it. My father, Baker Brand, was not in my life very much. He was a carpenter and he worked for other people, making them furniture or helping them to build a house. He wasn’t around a lot, and Mother never talked about him with any great love or affection. I found him hard to talk to and somewhat distant throughout the time he lived with us before my parents got a divorce. Basically, I think my mother just felt that he didn’t know how to take care of and support a family.

Before we left West Turin, my mother gave birth to my younger sister, Bessie, when I was not quite two years old. We were so near in age that we truly grew up together with a close bond. Because I was the older, I sometimes took on a motherly role with her, but mostly we just played together.

I have some memories of the train and boat rides we took to get to Minnesota. Sarah Etta, Bessie and I tended to stick together with Sarah Etta taking on the motherly role with her two younger sisters. It became a “grand adventure” for the three of us.

Clarria was still a baby when we left, and we stopped first in Wisconsin, where my parents had once considered staying. But Clarria died there in October 1865, not long after we arrived, and Mother did not want to remain in Wisconsin, so we moved on to Faribault, Minnesota. Once there, we seemed to settle down a little bit. Mother gave birth to two more girls — Effie Bee and Flora Emma — but Flora only lived for six months. My mother had been 41 years old when Flora was born and after Flora’s death I think she decided that enough was enough.

Therefore, by October of 1872, after the death of little Flora, our family was not going to grow any more. I had two older brothers — Samuel Perkins and Leonard William — and one older sister — Sarah Etta. Younger than me was Effie; we had lost Bessie only two months before.

I looked up to Sarah Etta and we often talked about some day going to a big city and making a lot of money. Sometimes it seemed like that was all my mother and father argued about: money. There was never enough, according to my mother, and my father never seemed to have the spirit to argue with her. He liked doing his carpentry and he was a quiet man, but he didn’t truly support us. Sarah Etta and Mother were always talking about ways that they could make money — and going to a big city to do it was the definite plan. They had watched Grandpa Higby buy and sell land often in West Turin, and it made him pretty wealthy. They thought they might be able to do the same thing. But they had to find a way to make money first in order to buy land.

We lived in Richland in Rice County, Minnesota. I was too young to remember West Turin as well as Sarah Etta could, but Richland became the town that I considered my childhood home. Nearby Faribault was the county seat, and we often went there for shopping and getting other necessities. But it was quiet in Richland and I liked that. Richland is also close to Waseca which is where my oldest brother, Samuel, and his wife, Martha, lived after they were married. Waseca was about 25 miles south of us in Richland, but we didn’t see them often.

The saddest and most difficult part of my life in Richland was when my little sister, Bessie, died so suddenly in a tragic accident on the farm. Mother blamed my father for Bessie’s death because he had allowed Bessie to ride a horse in front of the reaper. This happened in August of 1872, and I think it was clearly the moment when my mother decided that she could not tolerate my father any longer. Still, it took another two years to accomplish that.

In 1874, after 26 years of marriage, my parents divorced. This was something that my mother had wanted to do for many years. After Aunt Clarinda’s impossible situation, my mother was determined she would not go down the same path. She bided her time and waited for some of the laws to change — which they did. Aunt Clarinda would not have been able to get a divorce except if her husband had committed adultery, but by 1874 the laws allowed other reasons, and my mother could finally divorce my father. My father immediately left the area after their divorce, and my mother was now free, but Sarah Etta and I knew that she would need help to keep us all fed and dressed.

On 23 January 1876, I got married to William T. Larraman. He was my first love. Although he was older than me by six years, he had been the big brother of a friend of mine, and we loved each other so much that we enjoyed a close relationship and I suddenly found myself pregnant. I was 14 and William was 20. My mother was very upset when she learned I was pregnant but she felt strongly that we should marry so that the child would be legitimate. And so we married. I did love Bill, but I was quite young to have a child and, unfortunately, my little boy died on the same day he was born.

Bill was pretty devastated by the loss of our child, and so he left for a while, trying to find work, but he always came back. By then, my sister, Sarah Etta, had already gone to Kansas City to begin to find a way to earn money for herself and for the family. She wrote letters back to us and I was mesmerized by those letters, telling us about all that she was doing in Kansas City. I wanted to go there, too, and not only work with her, but also see if I could find out what I wanted to do to also earn a living. But before I could do that, Sarah Etta found herself in a difficult predicament, one that she couldn’t fix.

In late 1878, my beautiful and talented sister became pregnant, and unlike my situation she was unable to marry the father of her child. She wrote to Mother and told her what had happened. I know that Mother was angry, but she adored Sarah Etta, so she was prepared to help her in any way that she could. Sarah Etta remained in Kansas City until she could no longer hide her pregnancy. Then she came to live with us. As her time grew near, she and Mother went down to our older brother’s place in Waseca, and her little girl, Gracie, was born there. Samuel and his wife, Martha, were willing to take in Gracie. They already had one child, Alline, but Martha welcomed Gracie as her own.

After leaving the baby with Sam and Martha, Sarah Etta and I headed for Kansas City. Sarah Etta was anxious to get back to work and to attend to her financial situation. I wanted to be there to help whenever I could — and also earn money for myself and my family, especially Mother. It was the beginning of a very different life for me. I was a grown-up with major responsibilities and I was ever so excited to go to Kansas City.

item.title: Book 2: Sarah Ann
item.description:
Chapter 8: Looking Back

Today, I celebrate my 62nd birthday — 5 February 1893. I don’t know how many years I have left, but it’s been a life full of extremely difficult and emotional lows as well as wonderful highs, especially with my children.

My mother and father — Tryphena Perkins Higby and Abijah Isaac Higby — had a strong influence on me. My mother gave birth ten times to bring me and my siblings into the world. Not all of us survived — Cyrus, just two months old; Clarinda, dying amongst criminals; Norman, just four months old; Salmon, just a year old; James Knox, lost to us when he was only 28 years old; and little Kay, just two years old when she passed.

I was my mother’s 5th child, her second daughter, and I have thus far outlived six of my siblings with only brothers left: Samuel Perkins, Jared Stratton, and Andrew Jackson. My brothers have remained in West Turin, New York, where all of us were born, but after Clarinda’s terrible ordeal, I could no longer live there. My mother, completely crushed by what happened to Clarinda, died just six years after Clarinda — in 1867. My father remarried but he also soon gave in, passing away just four years after my mother — in 1871.

Growing up in West Turin was not all bad and difficult, but my sister and I figured out from a fairly early age that girls were not treated the same as boys. I saw this unfairness on a daily basis with my brothers — particularly Samuel and Jared — getting far more freedom to do what they wanted to do than Clarinda and I had. Watching them grow up, I knew they were going to find life just generally easier for them than it was for us women.

As Clarinda’s marriage fell apart and she attempted to end it, I saw her struggles and understood how desperate she was. I talked to my father and to Baker, my husband, to try to figure out how I could help Clarinda. But the laws were never on her side. I was afraid she might do something rash — and I kept trying to tell her that she must not do anything to harm James. I was hoping, somehow, that I could help her find a way to end her marriage yet keep her children. No matter what I did, however, her situation just got worse with every passing day. Ultimately, her decision to murder James was hers alone, but I felt guilty about it, believing that perhaps I might have done something to make her believe that she had no other option. Attending her trial was one of the most difficult things I have ever done and I knew that she would probably not avoid prison time.

After her conviction, living in West Turin became almost impossible. But I remained at first, hoping that I might be able to help with an appeal. During that time, I was unable to successfully carry a child to full term, and I lost a boy, Cassius, in 1862, just two years after Clarinda’s death. Before I convinced Baker to leave West Turin, I gave birth to two beautiful daughters: Julia Harriet and Bessie. Once I had convinced Baker that we had to leave, I felt tremendous relief that I no longer had to endure the stares and innuendoes that I experienced every time I went to town to buy something.

Like Clarinda, I didn’t want to remain married to Baker, but I was determined to wait until the right moment. As laws began to change, I knew my chance at divorce was coming closer every single day. And it finally came. After our divorce, Sarah Etta headed for Kansas City to try to find a life for herself — she was never going to end up like her Aunt Clarinda — and to help out with the family’s finances.

Unfortunately, although laws had improved for women, they had not changed a great deal. Deciding to work as a fancy lady and then to own her own establishment was genius on Sarah Etta’s part. If she had not fallen in love and found herself pregnant, perhaps her life would have been quite different. But I have learned that there is no point in crying over spilled milk — what will be will be. Sarah Etta did a remarkable job of taking care of herself and helping out her family as well. But she never got over the loss of her baby’s father and the fact that she couldn’t have Gracie with her in Kansas City.

Since her death, Julia and I have tried hard to make Gracie’s life not just “good” but we wanted her to have a chance to do something with her life. After Sarah Etta’s death and after we had settled the messy will, Julia and I concentrated on Gracie. We made sure that she will finish school and we hope that she is going to become a nurse; that is what she says she is interested in.

Several years ago, I met a man named John Kell. When I met him, he was still married to someone else, but his wife died in 1891. We were married on 10 November 1892. This has not been the same marriage I had with Baker. First of all, we are beyond worrying or thinking about having children. I am glad that part of my life is over. John and I are “equal” in all ways. We keep our finances separated; we both support ourselves. We enjoy doing things together — something that Baker and I rarely did. I don’t know how many years I have left, but marriage to John was a good decision.

So on my 62nd birthday, it is easy to look back and see the good things — and the pain of loss. I would have wished that my beautiful Sarah Etta and Bessie would have lived longer, but I still have Julia and Effie.

item.title: Book 2: Sarah Ann
item.description:
Chapter 7: The Will

From the time of her accident until her death in early 1890, my darling daughter, Sarah Etta, was in terrible pain. She often cried and called out for her little daughter, Gracie, who was still living with her aunt and uncle in Pierre, South Dakota. Watching my daughter live with such terrible pain was just barely bearable for me. Her death came as a relief because now she was at peace.

Within days of the funeral, of course, I learned about her will, which was not the one that I thought she had written. While in severe pain after her accident, she managed to write a new will and have it witnessed and signed without my knowledge or her sister Julia’s. We were both immediately shocked when we learned from the lawyer what it said.

The Kansas City Times, January 31, 1890

Sarah Etta’s will, signed October 20, 1888, opened with the standard instructions to pay her debts and funeral costs, then moved quickly into a long list of bequests to family and friends. Her father, Baker Brand, received just five dollars — a striking contrast to the hundred dollars she left each of her brothers, S.P. and Leonard W.H. Brand, and her sisters, Julia H. Laramore1 and Effie B. Pierpont. But that was no surprise because Sarah Etta was not happy with her father. She gave me, Sarah Ann Brand, a life interest in the rents and income from the house at 920 Woodland Ave., on condition that I keep it in good repair and current on taxes; upon my death, the property was to pass permanently to the Children’s Home on Charlotte Street. A number of friends and household associates were also remembered, including Mrs. B. Winters (two French statues) and Mrs. Lorna De Camp (her choice of household items or clothing, plus her largest diamond ring, worn on her forefinger). Mrs. A. Drummond and two coloured workers in her employ, Mrs. Georgia Brown and Annie Smith, were each to receive cash and the right to select items from her household goods or wardrobe.

The most detailed provision by far concerned her resort on Third Street and her daughter, Gracie. Sarah Etta left the use, rents, and income of this property to Mary Cannon (also known as Georgia Thomas) for as long as Cannon remained single, on the condition that Cannon pay $50 a month toward Gracie’s education and clothing, keep the property insured, and keep the taxes paid. Upon Cannon’s death or marriage, the property was to pass outright to Gracie. Sarah Etta also left a diamond brooch to Georgia Thomas, and her sealskin cloak, along with the rest of her wardrobe not otherwise given away, to Gracie. A $2,000 debt against the Woodland Ave. property, owed to John A. Moore, was to be paid off from the estate. C.W. Chase received her largest solitaire diamond ring.

Whatever remained of her diamonds, jewelry, and general estate was to be converted to cash. That money was to be used first to buy a burial lot at Union Cemetery and pay for a $300 monument at her grave, with the balance going to me, Sarah Ann Brand. She named David Phillips of Kansas City as her executor.

Finally, she added a contingency: if Gracie Cuba Brand should die without legitimate children, the property set aside for her would instead go to the Children’s Home — the same institution that would receive the house on Woodland after my death.

❦   ❦   ❦

Julia and I were immediately horrified to learn of this will and we knew that we would have to contest it. There was no other choice. First of all, we wanted to protect little Gracie, Sarah Etta’s daughter. As well, of course, Sarah Etta had been helping to support all of us, and we were certain that she would never have done this if she had been in her right mind. But the accident, resulting in terrible long-term pain, and the use of morphine to control it, were the cause of her distorted vision of the world. We knew that this was wrong, so we began immediately to speak to a lawyer and make arrangements to contest the will. We were angry with the lawyer who wrote up this will, as well, because we believed that he absolutely knew that Sarah Etta had lost her mind. All he wanted was his fee for writing up another will.

The Pettis County Courthouse in Sedalia, where the trial was held. (Courtesy of CourthouseHistory.com)

The trial for contesting the will finally arrived and Julia and I were quite nervous and apprehensive about it. Here’s what finally happened:

We brought suit to overturn the will, naming the housekeeper and the city’s orphan home as the primary defendants — the two parties who stood to inherit in the family’s place. The central legal question was simple to state and hard to prove: had my dear daughter, Sarah Etta, been of sound mind when she made her will, or had illness, drugs, and possibly the housekeeper’s influence robbed her of true judgment? Jury selection alone took the better part of a day, as lawyers on both sides worked to exclude anyone with prior experience in will disputes.

Their lawyer called witnesses who had done business with Sarah Etta for years — a saloon keeper who’d known her nearly a decade, an insurance agent who’d handled her real estate — and each testified to the same thing: her judgment in financial and business matters never wavered, before or after her injury. The saloon keeper had personally witnessed the will’s signing and saw nothing amiss in her manner that day or afterward.

Then our lawyer called her longtime doctor, who had treated her after her serious carriage accident years earlier. He described her growing dependence on morphine — starting at fractions of a grain and climbing, by the time of her death, to doses that would be considered enormous. He testified plainly that in the period surrounding when the will was written, she was, in his professional opinion, insane — swinging between apparent competence and delusion, particularly fixated on the belief that her own family wanted her dead so they could seize her property. He connected this directly to both her physical injuries and the drug used to manage them, and noted that both morphine and alcohol were known in his experience to erode family bonds specifically.

A parade of merchants and seamstresses who’d served her for years took the stand next, and, for me, their testimony had a strange, almost gothic consistency: Sarah Etta had bought compulsively and erratically, ordering elaborate gowns she’d never wear, hoarding dozens of dress patterns and untouched silk dresses in storage trunks, having one gown built heavy enough with beadwork that “no man on the jury could have worn it.” One witness described being summoned to fit Sarah Etta for a dress meant only for her own burial. Several noted she required morphine injections just to stand still long enough to be measured. More than one witness broke down or nearly fainted on the stand describing her volatility.

Both Julia and Effie, my two younger daughters, gave the most emotionally fraught testimony — Julia, dressed in black, spoke with obvious grief about years spent guarding Sarah Etta’s interests and watching the accident and the morphine remake her personality; she held up well under questioning. But my poor Effie collapsed in tears during cross-examination and had to be excused from the stand entirely, never returning to testify further. A hired nurse who’d cared for her in her final illness was prevented from giving her opinion on Sarah Etta’s mental state — the court sustained an objection before she could answer.

After a week of testimony, and one night where the jury reported themselves deadlocked, they returned the following morning and found in favour of us: the document, therefore, was declared not to be a valid will. Interestingly, before delivering that verdict, one juror asked the court to clarify who Gracie Cuba Brand was — she was identified as a niece, the daughter of my son, Samuel. Julia and I were determined to make sure that little Gracie was always protected from the scourge of gossip about illegitimate children.

The Kansas City Star, May 27, 1891, page 1

❦   ❦   ❦

After living through my dear sister Clarinda’s ordeal, and then watching my beautiful daughter, Sarah Etta, also deal with the usual male dislike for independent women, I was determined that my granddaughter, Gracie, would have all the opportunities we could give to her. Because Gracie had been mentioned in the will, I felt her rights had to be defended at the trial. So I hired a lawyer to work on her behalf and I telegrammed my son, Samuel, and told him that Gracie had to come to Kansas City immediately. He and his wife, Martha, were reluctant to send Gracie to me, but I insisted and they knew they couldn’t really change anything. They were living in Pierre, South Dakota, at the time, where my son worked as a carpenter. Martha accompanied Gracie, who was now 11 years old, as far as Minnesota (where they had once lived in Waseca), and then Julia had gone north to meet Gracie and accompany her to Kansas City.

Gracie, age 10 (left), with Alline Brand and Martha E. Brand. Gracie thought they were her sister and her mother; they were really her cousin and her aunt.

When I met Julia and Gracie at the train station, I was amazed at how much Gracie had grown and how beautiful she was becoming — just like her mother. But she was very different from her mother in one other way: while her mother was outgoing and constantly active, Gracie was quiet and reserved and almost fearful. She understood little about what was going on, and Julia and I tried to protect her from some of the gossip which was occurring ever since Sarah Etta had died and news of her will had been published in the paper. Everyone wanted to know who this “Gracie Cuba Brand” was, including the jury at the trial.

We didn’t let Gracie attend the trial, but the lawyer I had hired would protect her interests there. Instead, we got Gracie enrolled in school and, whenever possible, Julia or I would drop by the school to pick her up. She went to Woodland School, at 711 Woodland, just two blocks from Sarah Etta’s house at 920 Woodland, where Julia and I had been staying since her accident. We were pleased that the school was so close by. Gracie was quite lost and confused at first, but getting her into school and keeping her occupied helped her to adjust. She finished Grade 7 there and then moved on to Central High School, which was at the corner of 11th Street and Locust. She had to walk ten blocks west and then one block south. My darling Sarah Etta was gone, but her daughter began to thrive and I was so proud of her.

item.title: Book 2: Sarah Ann
item.description:
Chapter 6: The Accident

Not too long ago, I found the journal that my daughter, Sarah Etta Brand, had written, telling about her life up until Thanksgiving of 1885 when she was involved in a terrible carriage accident at 6th and Broadway in Kansas City.

She and Prince were running errands, I guess, and the streets were bustling with activity because of the Thanksgiving holidays. I have learned as well that this area underwent a massive transformation as streets were ripped up to build a new cable car system. It became a bottleneck zone, especially for horse-drawn carriages competing with cable cars. Sarah Etta was undoubtedly impatient, a trait I had noticed in her even as a very young girl. Prince was startled by something and reared up, causing the carriage to lunge forward. Sarah Etta was thrown out of the carriage and fell to the ground. In the confusion of that moment, the wheel of a large nearby dray rolled over her hips and she screamed in agony and terror. At that moment, her life changed forever.

Julia sent me a telegram — I was still living in Rice County, Minnesota — to tell me of this terrible accident. I knew right away that she’d be dealing with difficult health issues for months, so I packed my bags and headed to Kansas City. Both Julia and I nursed her for months. I purchased a small house in Excelsior Springs and I went there a few times each week while Julia took over the nursing duties. Julia and Sarah Etta lived together, as a matter of necessity, at Sarah Etta’s house at 920 Woodland Avenue.

❧   ❧   ❧

A 19th-century morphine kit

Sarah Etta was in such great pain that she needed morphine almost constantly. The doctors would inject it, and then she learned how to do it herself. The use of morphine was habitual with her from the time she commenced using it and the quantity increased from the first. At the beginning, the doctor told me that she took from one-half to three-fourths of a grain, and towards the last she took from three to four grains. I didn’t understand this term “grains” but I knew that she was increasing her usage. Between the terrible injury itself, which caused constant pain, and the increasing use of morphine, it was difficult to watch her slow descent into madness. From June 1888 to January 1890, when she died, she was, in my view, insane. Her mind was impaired and she did such crazy things. Many people with whom I talked also confirmed my feelings. The whole situation was, for Julia and me, almost unbearable.

For instance, she started wearing heavy winter clothing in the middle of the summer. I first noticed the change in the spring of 1888, when I found her in a towering rage and tried to quiet her. She seemed to be under the impression that Julia and I wanted her out of the way to “get her stuff.” The injury she sustained or the use of morphine to which she was addicted — or a combination of both — was clearly causing her extreme physical and mental distress.

❧   ❧   ❧

Julia and I worried constantly about her and we did everything we could to help her get through this ordeal, though neither of us could quite imagine how that would happen. After all the years she had lived in Kansas City, she knew a lot of people and frequented the same stores. Everyone noticed how changed she had become.

She was a frequent visitor at the firm of Bullene, Moore, Emery & Co., for instance, and she got to know some of the clerks better than others. After her accident, she often purchased large quantities of items and left them to be delivered — and many were never delivered. Many people thought she was insane and expressed their concern to me and to Julia. I was told that she would come into the store in an excited manner and rush from one part of the store to the other, looking at goods, never stopping very long to examine them and ordering nearly everything she took a fancy to. She was a fairly good buyer before she received her injury and the change in her manner after the injury was very marked.

A dress trimmed with jet

She also often went to A.N. Sloss’ millinery establishment — she loved this shop which was located at 1117 Main Street. It had been opened in 1879, and Sarah Etta had gone to Kansas City just four years before. The clerks in that store knew Sarah Etta by her professional name, Kitty Brown. Sometimes clerks from this store would come to Sarah Etta’s house to measure her for a dress. Sarah Etta gave one clerk an order for a dress trimmed with twenty-five pounds of jet. It was so heavy that it would have been impossible to wear. No one could convince her that it was a huge waste of money.

A Saratoga trunk

I found one day in Sarah Etta’s bedroom a Saratoga trunk which contained from 100 to 200 dress patterns and she had a wardrobe which contained thirty fine silk dresses that she had never worn. She said she never expected to wear any of the dresses she had in the trunk except a black satin one, which she wanted to be buried in. When she was being measured for a dress, she had to have two injections of morphine just to stand long enough to have her measurements taken.

❧   ❧   ❧

I was so worried about her. She was sane on some subjects and crazy on others. I just knew that her mind was unsound. She would yell at me and at Julia and every day was a trial to deal with her. Julia and I arranged for her to go to several hot springs in the area in the hope that that would relieve some of her pain. Julia and I worked with her doctor, Dr. Halley, who had been called in to see her right after the accident. Another doctor, Dr. Michaels, also tried to help. They both took care of her at the beginning. At one point Dr. Halley thought to perform an operation but Sarah Etta was so upset when discussing it that he decided against it.

Sometimes store attendants came to the house where Julia and Sarah Etta were living and tried to arrange orders for her. Mrs. M.J. Jacobs was a dressmaker whom Sarah Etta had first worked for when she came to Kansas City, but she told me after Sarah Etta’s accident that she considered her insane. She said that Sarah Etta was disturbingly variable in giving an order — and the next day she would countermand it and say she had never given an order the previous day. She even told me that she was a little bit afraid of her — she commented that the expression in her eyes and her general actions bothered her.

❧   ❧   ❧

St. Mary’s Church, where Sarah Etta’s funeral was held

Sarah Etta could be mean to both Julia and me, but we understood that she was no longer in her right mind. Sarah Etta and I had had a great bond for years, but this terrible accident changed everything. Every night I went to sleep disturbed by the agony she was in. I couldn’t see how it could possibly ever end well — and it didn’t. She was admitted to hospital and a few days later she passed on January 27, 1890. She was 36 years 9 months old — my truly lovely and beautiful daughter. Her funeral was Thursday, January 30, 1890, at 2 pm at St. Mary’s Church at the corner of 13th and Holmes. I didn’t want to lose my daughter — I have lost enough children already — but I was glad that she was no longer in pain and she was hopefully at peace. But I had to consider another person now: Sarah Etta’s daughter, Grace. I had promised Sarah Etta that I would make sure her daughter was taken care of and eventually knew who her mother was.

However, on the day of the funeral, I had no idea what battle was yet to come.

Sarah Etta’s death notice in the Kansas City Star. (The paper had her age wrong; she was 36.)

item.description:
Chapter 5: Life in Kansas City without Grace

After my little Gracie was born, I stayed with my brother and sister-in-law for a couple of months, wishing that I could take her back with me to Kansas City. I knew it wasn’t going to happen, but I wanted to have her with me. However, I could never convince my brother and his wife, nor my mother, that it was a good idea, so I finally gave up begging and returned to Kansas City without her. I had a business to run.

Within two years after returning, I purchased a second resort — this one on Third Street. I am busy going back and forth between my two resorts now, but I am definitely making a lot of money — enough to support me, to purchase clothes and jewelry, and to help support my mother, siblings, and my daughter as well. I have acquired a lot of lovely things, including a sealskin coat — which is great for Kansas City winters — and a beautiful diamond brooch.

Since returning to Kansas City, I haven’t been quite the same. Losing my lover, leaving behind my child, I have struggled to find meaning and purpose. I still want my independence and I still want to support and help my mother and my little sister, Effie. But I know that something is missing from my life. I fill the emptiness with alcohol and driving as fast as I can whenever I can.

❖   ❖   ❖

My horse, Prince, is a Morgan. I purchased him as soon as I could afford a horse and carriage. There are many places nearby my resort where I could board him and my carriage, but there is a very convenient one right across the street from my resort on Third Street, so I can easily go back and forth and see my horse.

Prince is a gelding with a refined head and a long neck. He is lean and athletic, not like a draft horse, and his legs are longer and finer than a draft horse. He can go fast and his endurance seems much greater than my own! I like him to be well-groomed and I often go to his stable and brush him and talk to him. I bought a bridle with blinders, which helps Prince to stay focused in traffic. I use a breast-collar harness rather than a heavy draft collar, and a saddle pad which supports the shafts of the buggy.

Sarah Etta in her buggy

I bought a buggy that I knew would be fast. It is high-wheeled and is considered a light road buggy. It was designed for personal transportation rather than for farm hauling. It has four large spoked wheels and a very light frame. I like the seating position, which is high and allows me to see very far ahead. The bench is a little narrow and there’s not much side support, but that makes it lighter in weight and therefore easier for Prince to pull me. That carriage is built for speed, lightness and style rather than for stability. I don’t mind that because I really love getting in that carriage and letting Prince go as fast as he can.

Some people told me that I was crazy to have such a light wagon without much support, but I love the speed I can achieve with it. Whenever I get upset and down, missing my little Grace, I enjoy getting in that buggy and giving Prince free rein. Of course, that sometimes means that I am fined for “fast driving” and it’s true that I often like to drink before I take Prince out. But it’s just too much fun to do. When I am riding in that carriage with Prince galloping as fast as he can, I think only of the speed and the excitement.

A while back, a newspaper reported on one of my races:

A very prominent official of this place, who owns a 2:40 racer, participated in a race the other day with Miss Kitty Brown of Kansas City. The race was very exciting, going through the north end of town at locomotive speed. When near the bridge down brakes was sounded, and Miss Brown was victorious.

I love it when things like that get in the paper — it certainly doesn’t hurt my businesses either.

❖   ❖   ❖

I do enjoy those fast rides, but I also have a business to run, and I have been busy earning money, buying more places, and making sure my resorts are clean, healthy, and respectable places. There are many resorts in the area so I have to do something to make my resort unique. The outside of the buildings are all simple and straightforward: brick and mortar, mostly. But inside I want it to be classy, perhaps even opulent.

Both of my houses look much like a residential-style building, both of them have two floors. The ground floor is the public and social space; the upper floors are where the private rooms are located. In both houses, I have 12 private rooms upstairs, each simply furnished with a bed, a washstand and basin, and a mirror.

The parlour truly is the heart of the whole process. I have furnished it to project an image of respectability and comfort including upholstered furniture, rugs, mirrors, and a piano. It is in the parlour where the girls and I entertain the clients. I didn’t have a liquor license at first, but I finally got one in July of 1884 and that helped to bring more men to my resorts (however, I had been selling it illegally before that). In the parlour we serve drinks and encourage conversation. Annie Chambers charges $5 a bottle for wine so I charge only $4. I expect my girls to encourage the men to drink — just another way to make more money.

Of course, my girls live there all the time. They eat their meals together and spend a lot of their off-hours right there at the resort. I go back and forth between the two places quite a bit, but I always have quarters for myself: in both places my room is on the ground floor, which allows me to know all the comings and goings of the entire house. Recently, I also purchased a house on Woodland Avenue — this is a simple residential home, not a resort.

I always liked my girls to be as well dressed as I was.

The parlour is genuinely important to the success of my resorts. An evening might begin with a client being admitted into the parlour; girls would begin to join him and more men would arrive. My girls are always dressed elegantly. I don’t want their clothes to be too revealing, but enough to entice the customers. Conversation, music, and drinking might go on for some time before any private arrangement is concluded. I cultivate the situation deliberately, because it attracts a wealthier clientele who values the illusion of a social call as much as anything else.

Some of the other resorts even have entertainment that keeps clients in the building for longer. I don’t always do that, but sometimes I hire someone for a Friday or Saturday night. But I always have the absolute authority in the house. I control everything.

First, of course, I always know where the money is: This is fundamental. Women living in my resorts typically pay me for their room, board, clothing, and medical expenses — all deducted from their earnings. I am not as generous as Annie Chambers, who splits the income 50/50 with her girls; I split it 60/40. This system of debt can be very difficult to escape, since a woman might always owe more than she earns. Even Annie’s 50/50 arrangement keeps women financially tied to the house. So I try to counsel my girls and help them to use their money wisely.

I decide who enters the building, who is admitted to which women, and who is thrown out. I have a Negro man, William Stone, who helps out when we need to evict a rowdy customer or one who refuses to pay. But I will brook no nonsense from men who misbehave. William has worked for me for several years. Because he is a Negro, I can pay him less, but he’s usually reliable and I like him. Some of my girls don’t care for him, but I tell them to just stay away. He doesn’t mingle with the others in the parlour; I always tell him to stay out of sight as much as possible, but most of my customers just view him as a servant (which is close to what he is).

It is important to me that I control the reputation of my establishments. We need to be reputable and clean. I control what my women wear, how they speak to the clients, and how they behave in the parlour. A woman who can converse intelligently with a wealthy businessman is worth far more to the house than one who can’t. I worked my way up through the ranks and I understand exactly what standards are required.

Some medical control is also a practical necessity. Venereal disease is an ever-present threat, and I cannot allow sick women to work; that would quickly destroy my reputation and my business. I have a regular arrangement with a physician who examines the women periodically. Dr. Smith — like us, he uses a pseudonym — can be trusted to be discreet and confidential. He is employed by several madams, including myself and Annie Chambers.

My relationship with the police is perhaps the most critical thing I have to control. I am the one who pays the periodic fines, maintains the relationship with the ward politicians, and ensures the house operates within the understood — if unofficial — boundaries that keep us from being shut down. I know a lot of the police officers and we always try to behave well when they are around. My clients come from all walks of life and occupation — including politicians, policemen, lawyers, and judges.

Sometimes we have a little fun, too. Here’s a sample from one newspaper clipping:

As a grand finale, the fair Kitty Brown of Third Street, and her attendant handmaidens, made their appearance and softly murmur “guilty” to the charge of keeping and being inmates of a naughty house. It seems that some of the maidens went on a grand spree yesterday, while Kitty was asleep, and failing to find amusement indoors, resorted to the street, where they performed the Parisian can-can in attire that closely resembled Mother Eve’s previous to the apple episode. For this the house was raided and Kitty paid $25 while Carrie Eaton, Eva Porter, Martha Eaton, Stella Goodwin and Daisy Brown [yep — that’s my sister] each paid $5. This closed the entertainment.

I love it when articles like this get in the newspaper. It is great advertising for my resorts. By this time, my sister, Julia, had arrived and started using Daisy Brown as her professional name.

❖   ❖   ❖

So, after Gracie was born in 1879, I returned to KC and have now spent another five years here, increasing my income considerably, and helping everyone in my family. I love them — my mother, my brothers, my sisters — but sometimes it feels as though I am the one doing all the work. I hope against hope that some day I can have Grace with me — she is now six years old, and my mother tells me that my brother and his wife are thinking of moving to Pierre, in Dakota Territory, where they think that my brother can make more money as a carpenter. Sometimes he seems just like my father — always worrying and fretting about everything. I don’t like it that my daughter will be moving farther away from me. If I can just get through a few more years on my own, then I can have her join me here in Kansas City.

item.description:
Chapter 4: Love Found and Love Lost

It is difficult to tell this part of my story. After what happened to my Aunt Clarinda and witnessing my own parents’ divorce, I wasn’t sure that I would ever want to marry, never mind having children. The world just didn’t seem like a great place to try to bring up children, and I still felt that women had little power, especially married women. Although things had greatly improved since my aunt’s experience, it had been only twenty years since she had endured a marriage that was on the rocks and she was totally unable to extricate herself from that marriage and keep her children.

Cuba

But affairs of the heart are not always easily controlled and, despite my determination to remain unmarried and totally in control of my life and finances, I met someone. He came to my place on Grand Avenue, as this was before I had purchased the place on Third Street. There seemed to be an instant attraction and we hit it off immediately. He came to see me week after week after week and we spent hours talking about his life, his work, and — yes — his family. He had left behind in Cuba a wife and one small child, as his wife did not want to leave. He insisted that he didn’t mind what I did for a living and, in fact, he admired me for being different and not just following traditional roles.

He had come to America to escape the war against Spain and continue making a living and send money home to his wife and child. Cuba was trying to get its independence from Spain and some Cubans left the country rather than live in a difficult situation. Personally, I didn’t care much for a cigar, although I smoked one occasionally — which is something women didn’t generally do. It is my understanding that the 1870s were like a “golden age” for cigar smoking, and this was primarily because of the war in Cuba.

Cuban men came to the United States and established cigar manufacturing places. My lover was one of those men, and he built a cigar-making company near my resort on Grand Avenue. Cigar factories seemed to be everywhere and they could be simply a person in a room rolling cigars or a factory of men and women making them. Kansas City seemed like a great place to establish a factory, just as I had seen it as a great place for me to make my own fortune. With businessmen and cowboys coming and going daily, it was easy to sell a lot of things, including sex and cigars. Obtaining the tobacco for the cigars was a bit difficult, as it had to be shipped to Kansas City, but he felt that the market was so good for selling them that it offset the cost of getting the tobacco there. Cuban tobacco was considered the best, and Cuban men who came to the US to sell Cuban cigars would advertise them as Havana cigars.

Havana cigars

The war disrupted cigar production on the island of Cuba, resulting in more and more Cuban cigar makers moving to the American market. My lover and friend did not join the large Cuban communities in New York and Florida, but he was well known in Kansas City because there weren’t as many Cubans in the city. During the July 4th parade in 1878, many people marched, showing off all of the city’s successes, including those who owned and operated cigar factories!

One factory, operated by H. Tobner and Brothers, was one of the oldest in the city. They had establishments in three places along Grand Avenue — one of them very close to my first resort — and they made cigars as well as chewing and smoking tobacco. I was told by my lover that they employed over 45 people and they could make 80,000 cigars in a week.

I learned many things from this man and he became an important part of my day. Before long, he was coming to visit almost daily, usually in the late afternoon or early evening. The biggest problem I had after several months of his friendship was figuring out how to not fall in love with him. But I did anyway. I told myself that this was all a bad idea, that he might not stay, that he might return to Cuba, and that he was married and had a child. Still, the love grew stronger and our desire to be together became obvious to all who knew us.

♥   ♥   ♥

In 1873, just two years before I arrived in Kansas City, Congress passed a law known as the Comstock Act. It defined contraceptives as obscene and illicit, making it a federal offense to disseminate birth control through the mail or across state lines. This was just, in my estimation, another way for men to control women, but the effect of the law was immediate. Medical advice books on anatomy, contraception, pregnancy, and childbirth were taken out of libraries. Druggists warned customers that small packages would be examined at post offices. Condoms and diaphragms became harder to find and ads for abortionists disappeared from newspapers.

After what had happened to my Aunt Clarinda, I wasn’t going to just sit back and let men, once again, tell me what I could do with my body. As a working girl, never mind after I became the boss, I knew about various techniques, and I taught these ideas to my girls.

Some of the things we could do included condoms or douching or both. I usually made condoms from linen for myself and my girls, and we often added an ointment, hopefully to prevent the clap or the pox. Believe it or not, there were laws against the use of them, and some clients didn’t like them, but my girls and I were willing to use them when we could. Douching had been used as a means of birth control for about 30 years before I even came to Kansas City. Sometimes solutions such as vinegar and alum were used with syringes. This was very popular with my girls because we could control it.

There were birth control devices, of course, despite the laws, including vaginal suppositories, syringes sold with acidic solutions for douching, and antiseptic spermicides. These were methods we could use without the knowledge of the men. Medical guides often recommended different types of teas that were typically used not as preventatives but as an early way to abort a baby. I had heard some terrible tales about this technique, including death if the herbs were misused, so I tended to discourage my girls from using them.

Perhaps one of the more common techniques was a simple withdrawal before the final moment. Not a lot of my customers liked that, so it was hard to control. The most popular method — for my mother, for me, and for my girls — was the rhythm method. We knew when we had had our periods and we knew when we would be the most fertile. The advantage of having numerous women in a resort is that some of them, on any given day, might feel that this was not a good day for them to take a chance on getting pregnant. I always told my girls that they could take days off to protect themselves from pregnancy.

♥   ♥   ♥

At some point in my relationship with my lover, I got a bit too casual, and sometime in late 1878 I discovered that I was pregnant. At first, I wasn’t sure what I wanted to do, but then I finally got my courage up to tell my lover what had happened. Much to my dismay and disappointment, he told me that he would not and could not marry me, that he was returning to his wife and child in Cuba, and that I would have to fend for myself. I did not expect him to desert me; I was devastated.

I wrote to my mother immediately and I will say that my mother was wholly supportive and willing to help. She had some choice comments to make about my lover, who was deserting me, but she would never have suggested that I give up the baby or abort the pregnancy. So we began to plot and consider just what I was going to do. I remained in Kansas City and continued to work and to run my resort, trying to keep my pregnancy concealed from as many people as I possibly could. That was pretty easy; I spent most of my time in my establishment and didn’t see many people.

When I could no longer hide my pregnancy at about 7½ months, I found myself ready to move north and stay with my mother in Faribault. It was actually a fun time. My sister, Julia, was still living at home, and her husband, William T. Larraman, was living there with her. Now at age 17, she and I had a lot in common to talk about. She had lost her baby a few years before and she wanted to see me carry mine to term. Also still at home were my brother Leonard (age 24), my sister Effie (age 11), and one of my father’s cousins, Mattie (age 23). As my due date got closer, Mother and I travelled down to Waseca to be with my brother, Samuel, and his wife, Martha. I gave birth to my little girl in August of 1879. I named her Grace, which originates from the Latin gratia, which means “favour,” “blessing,” or “thanks.” In my view, it has always been one of the more popular virtue names; it represents divine love, mercy, and elegance. I gave her the middle name of Cuba so she would have a hint as to who her father was.

Grace was my love child, the daughter I had always wanted, and someone I could give all my love to. It nearly killed me when I had to leave her behind with my brother and sister-in-law instead of taking her back to Kansas City with me. She never knew who her father was — and he never saw her, spoke to her, or supported her.
