item.description:
Chapter 3: Life in Kansas City

In 1875, when I was 22, I travelled by train to Kansas City — but this time I was alone, not with my parents and my older and younger siblings. The train headed south through Iowa first and then reached Chicago; I then took a train southwest to Kansas City. It was a three-day trip; my mother was concerned that I was travelling alone, but I was determined to go even though it wasn’t common for women to travel alone. I was going to be my own person and make my own way in the world — without a husband. I think you could say that I was almost giddy with anticipation.

Kansas City was wonderful and I loved everything about it: the noise, the bustle, the activity, people coming and going. It was all such a delight. I started working for a woman who made clothes for the boarders who were in the “West Bottoms” area and, as I got to know these women, I realized that I might be able to find a more lucrative lifestyle as a fancy lady than as a dressmaker, but I took my time to figure out the situation and what might be the best way for me to earn an income.

A busy 4th Street in Kansas City in 1875.

After I arrived, I was curious about what was going on and why, trying to figure out how to make some money and be on my own. I had learned from my grandfather and my mother that one way to earn a living was to own property and rent it or sell it. Unlike the situation my aunt Clarinda was in just 15 years before, I now had the right to own and sell property. So, getting to know Kansas City and its various areas, how people earned money, and how I could make use of the world I was living in — all of that became important to me. It didn’t take long for me to understand some of the history of the area and why Kansas City was booming when I arrived. Essentially, I studied and listened and learned as much as I could about the area. If I was going to make my way in the world, I figured I could learn from others who had helped to develop Kansas City. I talked to the locals — people who had been living here for a while — and I even spent time checking out newspaper articles, too.

✦   ✦   ✦

Kansas City is virtually in the middle of the United States, where the longest river in the country, the Missouri, meets the Kansas. The Missouri River was like a lifeline for travellers, taking them all the way west as far as they could go by boat. It was way faster than traveling on land. But this particular bend in the river became a natural spot for travellers to rest and get ready for their next move. That’s where they built the Union Station and most of the bars and resorts — convenient for the men as they got off the train. This area became known as “The Bottoms” and it is where I would eventually spend most of my time.

In the very early days, French explorers from St. Louis had moved up the Missouri River, trapping for furs and trading with the local tribes. The United States bought this entire area from France in 1803; it was called the Louisiana Purchase, and people started settling there not long after that. But the area wasn’t settled by just one person. It took the efforts of many to make it boom.

Everyone knew about François Chouteau, for instance, a French fur trader who set up a trading post at the bend of the Missouri, but after a massive flood, he moved the post to the south bank near the foot of present-day Grand Avenue (which is where I would start my first business). It didn’t take me long to learn that flooding could be a major problem for Kansas Citians, especially if you lived near the river. I was concerned about what might happen to my property if a flood occurred.

Kansas City today, on both sides of the state line, with Westport and the Missouri and Kansas (Kaw) rivers. The arrows show which way the rivers flow. The enlarged box shows where Sarah Etta’s two houses stood, on Grand Avenue and at 4th and Wyandotte.

Westport was the first town in the area, established by a man named John McCoy. Like me, he saw the potential for earning a living here: he opened an outfitting store for pioneers who were heading down the Santa Fe Trail. He also built a riverboat landing on the bluffs at the bend in the Missouri River. Westport, therefore, became popular because it was close to Kansas Territory and because settlers and traders could trade with the Indian tribes who had been forced to move there in the 1830s.

In 1838, fifteen years before I was born, fourteen men decided to expand the town’s boundaries and grab some land along the river. They included Westport Landing in their plans, and in 1850, they officially became the Town of Kansas. The name Kansas City comes from the Kansas, or Kaw, River, which was named after the Kansa Indians. Later on, in 1853, the state of Missouri decided to incorporate the area as the City of Kansas, which is exactly what it was called when I first arrived.

Once the railroad arrived in Kansas City in 1865, it was like a magic wand that connected the city to all sorts of trade networks. This massive development really boosted Kansas City’s growth. But what really opened up the area was the Hannibal Bridge over the Missouri River, completed in 1869, just six years before I arrived. This bridge transformed Kansas City into a major transportation hub, and, despite the competition with some other cities, once the decision was made to build the bridge, it was obvious to me that it became the undisputed champion of the region.

In essence, geography played a huge role in developing Kansas City — and making it a great place for me to make a living. In the past, the river’s confluence made Kansas City an irresistible spot for Native peoples, then French traders, and finally, American settlers. Eventually, railroad investors couldn’t resist either, so each group built on what the previous one had accomplished. I just latched on to those stars and made my way.

✦   ✦   ✦

Kansas City was a real hotspot for travellers and many workers, especially men. When I arrived, Kansas City was at the height of the Texas cattle drives. The men arriving were not just railroad workers — they were trail bosses, cattle barons, and cowboys flush with money after months on the trail. Many of these men were anxious to drop by my establishment. They came in droves, and there were certain activities they liked to do best: gambling, drinking, and hanging out at saloons and houses around the old Union Depot in the West Bottoms area. The city’s railroad boom brought in all sorts of folks, like cowboys and westward migrants. Young, unmarried men outnumbered us women by a landslide, so they flocked to the 80 saloons and 40 houses of prostitution that catered to the bustling population of 50,000.

I figured out that many women hung out around military forts, trading posts, mining camps, and cattle towns, trading their bodies for some cash. It was a way for some women to escape the not-so-great jobs they had as laundresses, maids, and factory workers. In many cases, it was their only chance to make a living without family support or money. I was determined to use this business to make a name for myself and, in the meantime, I was also helping other women to find their independence.

By 1880 — when I had already purchased one resort and was hoping to buy another one soon — the city enacted its first “sin laws.” But by then, these resorts were well established, including Annie Chambers’ mansion at 201 West 3rd Street. Even though she was only a few blocks from police headquarters, her resort was never raided, nor was mine. My house was on the same block as hers, also facing Third Street. Annie was here a little before me and she became quite well known, but I truly think that most of the men liked my place better than hers. Annie had a bit of a sanctimonious attitude toward her girls, and she kept a tight ship. I had a few girls come to my place after they had been in Annie’s and they liked my style of leadership better than Annie’s. Mainly, I gave them more freedom than Annie did. City governments in the region actually profited from prostitution by fining my girls and me as the owner. The “sporting woman” was also seen as a necessary evil since she attracted potential business. And we did that — oh, yes indeed, we did that.

I quickly learned by observing others that I wanted to run a resort of my own — a place where my boarders would be safe. There were many different “arrangements.” At the top were the parlour houses — establishments like my resort, where the surroundings were luxurious, the women were well-dressed and well-versed in social graces, wine and cigars were served, and the prices reflected all of that. When I worked for another madam, I charged up to $10 and gave half to her; once I became the madam myself, of course, that arrangement reversed. I wanted my resorts to be beautiful and comfortable — a place where the clients could come and relax, rest, and have fun.

Once I had purchased a resort, my name began to appear in the papers when my girls and I were “arrested” and “fined” for having a “house of ill repute.” It became almost a joke, really, and it was, in many ways, free advertising: the newspaper comments brought me more customers.

By 1879, I was listed in Hoye’s directory, which listed people in Kansas City. Early on, I chose the name Kitty Brown as my professional name. It took time to purchase the things I wanted for my resort. I wanted comfortable but attractive furniture, a room where the men could relax and sit and talk, smoke their cigars, and perhaps get to know the girls. We were open at all times of the day and night, and I stayed there as much as I could. I wanted to be there if there was trouble and, alas, sometimes there was, simply because young men get drunk and sometimes get silly or jealous or angry.

From left to right: Kitty Brown’s establishment, a large private home, and Annie Chambers’ resort, which faced Third Street.

There were resorts like mine and Annie’s, but there were also just ordinary houses. They were decent enough, but they lacked the elegance and the high prices of resorts like mine. Then, there were these places called cribs and they were referred to as 25-cent houses. They were very small and cheap, sometimes just a single room with a door to the street. In these cribs, a woman would sit or stand in the doorway, trying to entice men inside. The women who worked in these cribs barely made ends meet. They often paid a lot of rent to the crib owner and lived in very poor conditions. It was a stark contrast to the parlour houses, and there was no way I was going to work in those conditions.

Because I eventually owned two resorts, I was at the upper end of this hierarchy. I wasn’t a crib worker or a streetwalker — heaven forbid. I was a businesswoman who accumulated enough capital to purchase real property. That was genuinely unusual and I showed that I was capable of making it on my own. In a world where most women in the trade ended up impoverished, sick, or dependent on a madam, I became the madam herself — and a property-owning one at that. I went from dressmaker to working girl in remarkably short order, and I met a lot of important people. It wasn’t just cowboys and dock workers who came to my place, even before I was the madam. Men of high rank — in politics, in the business world, in finance — also were my regular trade.

✦   ✦   ✦

Shortly before I purchased my first resort, however, I did the very thing I told my girls to never do: I fell in love with one of my clients. This was something I had not intended to do. However, he was tall, dark, and handsome, which is a bit of a cliché, but it was really true. I can still remember the first time he came into my resort: He was a bit shy but curious about me, my life, and how I lived. The first thing he told me was that he made Cuban cigars for a living, which didn’t seem like anything particularly exciting, but he had a slight Cuban accent, a quiet demeanour, and he treated me like a queen, bringing me gifts each time he came. His schedule was somewhat erratic, but he came to see me at least twice a week.

Unfortunately, he was also married. And, despite my efforts to prevent it, I found myself pregnant in late 1878. I wanted a child but I also wanted a husband. It was not a good situation for me or for my child — and I turned to my mother and sister for advice and help. All of my careful planning had not prepared me for this new twist.

Chapter 2: Good-bye, New York; Hello, Minnesota

After my aunt’s conviction and sentencing, everyone was devastated. My grandparents took care of my cousins: Linda (8), Almeda (7), Andrew (5), Benjy (3), and Eugenia (2). They were quiet, but the boys, Andrew and Benjy, showed signs of anger, unhappiness, and rebellion early on. Linda, Almeda, and Eugenia were more compliant and helpful. As they grew older, we lost track of them and it seemed like they almost disappeared.

Before my aunt’s struggles, my mother gave birth to five children: Samuel, Lafayette (who died at three), me, Leonard, and Susan (who lived only eight months). During my aunt’s trial, my mother was too stressed to carry a child to term. She gave birth to a boy in May 1860 who only lived two years. But after my aunt’s death in 1860, she gave birth in 1861 and 1863 — my two younger sisters, Julia and Bessie.

My mother was no different than many other women at this time. Having a child was dangerous — women often died of infection — and one in five babies didn’t live to be a year old. My aunt Clarinda had done well to give birth to five babies who all survived, while my mother lost some of hers. Babies and young children often got sick with cholera, tuberculosis, scarlet fever, diphtheria, measles, and whooping cough. I watched some of my little siblings die, and we didn’t always know what they were sick with, but we knew they were sick and we didn’t have a thing to give them to help them.

As time went on, my parents felt increasingly unable to stay in West Turin. My mother, in particular, faced negative gossip, and many believed she had helped my aunt murder her husband. Finally, she couldn’t take it anymore and told my father that we must move. I was relieved, as I’d also faced bullying and gossip at school. I loved my Aunt Clarinda, and being told I was the niece of a murderer devastated me. My mother repeatedly reminded me that Aunt Clarinda had been desperate and unhappy; she could turn to no one for help. She never said that it was all right for Clarinda to murder her husband, but she repeated often how desperate she was.

❦   ❦   ❦

In 1865, about two years after Bessie’s birth, we moved to Minnesota, following my father’s family’s decision to relocate there. My grandfather Brand had struggled financially, unlike my grandfather Higby. My father grew up on Tug Hill, a cold, wet, and isolated hill actually located in the city of West Turin. My grandparents met and married in England before coming to the US after my father and his older brother were born. In the early 1830s, my grandfather was offered a job on Tug Hill selling properties, and the family moved there when my father was seven. My grandmother Brand eventually gave birth to 14 children.

In 1850, my grandparents and many of their children moved to Fond du Lac, Wisconsin, where my grandfather tried to revive his trade as a butcher. My grandmother died there in 1855, and my grandfather remarried to a woman named Sarah Ann Bixby in 1858. My parents decided to move to Wisconsin, possibly reuniting with my father’s family. Another reason for leaving was the end of the Civil War — it might be safer to travel now that the war was over.

I was 11 years old when we began our trip. We left on a stagecoach to Rome, then boarded the New York Central Railroad’s Water Level Route. This was a 960-mile journey from New York City to Chicago which avoided the Appalachian Mountains by following rivers and lakeshores. It took about 12 hours, with a few train changes, but we usually stayed on the same train. I enjoyed looking out the window looking at the countryside — sometimes lots and lots of trees, other times rivers or lakes, and sometimes deep mountain canyons. It was more of the country than I had ever seen before, and I loved it. With each turn of the train’s wheels, we left West Turin and its gossip behind, and we looked forward to new faces, new ideas, new land.

As mentioned already, my parents initially planned to stop in Wisconsin and stay with my grandparents and cousins, perhaps to stay there permanently. Shortly after we arrived, however, my one-year-old sister Clarria became ill and passed away in Fond Du Lac. Mother had lost so many children — and she remained devastated by her sister’s death — that she could not face staying there where her daughter had died. She urged my father to move on and travel to Minnesota, which had always been part of the plan (we would move on from Wisconsin to Minnesota if things didn’t look promising in Wisconsin).

So, after some decision-making between my parents, we took another train to Faribault, Minnesota. The Minnesota Central, which started as the Minneapolis and Cedar Valley line, reached Faribault in 1865 and Owatonna in 1866, making Faribault the end of the line. It also extended south from Minneapolis through Faribault to Iowa, connecting Chicago and the Twin Cities through Wisconsin.

We arrived in Minnesota in January 1866, just as that train had even finished to Faribault. The train ride was exciting but challenging. The cars were sparse, with wooden benches, coal stoves, and no dining cars. We carried our own food, water, and bedding. At major transfer cities like Buffalo or Chicago, we sometimes had to change trains or stay overnight at a station hotel. There were still things to see outside the window, but the landscape of Minnesota was pretty unexciting and ordinary compared to the trees and hills of New York.

❦   ❦   ❦

It wasn’t easy for Mother to say goodbye to my grandparents, and she would’ve taken care of Clarinda’s children, but Father said it wasn’t possible. When we arrived in Minnesota, Samuel was 16 and Leonard was 8. I helped my mother with childcare, looking after Leonard and my two little sisters, Julia and Bessie. Julia, the older of the two, was closest to me and followed me everywhere. She only knew family stories because she was born after Aunt Clarinda’s death, but she was a good listener.

By the time we arrived in Minnesota, Mother had given birth nine times, and four of those children had died before they reached the age of four. Before we left West Turin, both Julia and Bessie were born and thrived. I really became their mother, helping them and teaching them all that I knew. But after we were settled on the Minnesota farm, Mother had two more children — two little girls, Effie and Flora. Flora lived only six months, but Effie survived those difficult infant years, and being the youngest, she clung to my mother’s apron strings for years. After Flora’s birth, my mother had no more children.

People back in West Turin always said we lived in one of the coldest, snowiest corners of New York, and they weren't wrong. Tug Hill (where my father lived) caught every storm that blew off Lake Ontario, and our winters were long and usually buried deep in snow. I thought I knew cold. But Minnesota cold was different. The wind came across those flat open plains with nothing to stop it and it cut right through you in a way the wet, heavy cold of West Turin never did. The summers, though, surprised me. Back in West Turin, summers were mild and short. In Faribault, they were hot and long, with thunderstorms that rolled in fast across a wide open sky. The springs were later than I expected and the autumns shorter. But it was the sky that struck me most — enormous and unobstructed in every direction, nothing like the view from the hills of West Turin.

Main Street, Faribault

The nearest town for us in New York was Constableville, and it was a modest place — a handful of general stores, two churches, a couple of hotels, and a small school. It served the farmers and lumbermen of the area well enough. Mother did most of her shopping there, and I walked to the schoolhouse with the other children from the surrounding farms. When we arrived in Faribault, I was surprised at how different it was from West Turin. The railroad had just come through, and the mills along the Straight River were running steadily. There were flour mills, a woolen mill, grain elevators, and more shops along the main street than I had ever seen in one place. The town even had schools for the deaf and the blind, and people called it the Athens of the West. The school I attended was better equipped than anything I had known in Constableville, and the town itself felt purposeful and forward-looking in a way that West Turin, for all its familiarity, never quite had. It felt so good to be away from people who knew about Aunt Clarinda. I actually looked forward to going to school!

❦   ❦   ❦

After my Aunt Clarinda’s tragic death, I thought we’d avoid more tragedies. My mother was used to losing babies, but another tragedy would end my parents’ marriage. In mid-August 1872, my father was harvesting the fall crops. He lacked farmhands, so most older kids, including Bessie, who had just had her ninth birthday, helped. (The newspaper article below says she was 10, but that is inaccurate.)

An article appeared in the paper the day after the terrible accident and it read as follows:

Girl maimed and killed by reaper.

From the Faribault Democrat of the 23rd of this month we get the following details of a terrible misfortune briefly mentioned earlier. The Democrat writes: in consequence of the shortage of labor it has been necessary among farmers in Rice County to enlist the aid of women and children in the work of harvesting, and the last named have been much used, as in the present case, in driving the draught animals of the reaper.

On Monday last, Bessie Brand, the 10 year old daughter of Father Brand, of Midlands Town, was riding the steer horse in front of a reaper, when it suddenly became unruly, went berserk and threw her straight in front of the reaper, which went over her, cutting off her left leg just above the ankle and her right arm above the elbow. On her right leg the flesh was cut off from the knee to the abdomen. She was also severely injured on the head and chest.

The accident happened at about 8 o'clock in the morning and the child lived for about 3 hours. She died before the doctor, who could not have done anything, came to her aid. The reaper was pulled by a pair of bulls, in front of which the steering horse was harnessed. Farmer Brand was sitting on the reaper and was thrown to the ground just in front of the blades. He only managed to escape his daughter's fate by the narrowest of margins. The injured girl was a lively, intelligent child and her terrible fate spread grief throughout the neighbourhood.

I was worried my mother would die after Bessie’s death. It was a needless and agonizing loss, and she couldn’t bear being near my father. She blamed him entirely. The laws had finally changed from when Aunt Clarinda had wanted a divorce, and so, in 1874, my parents divorced after going to Massachusetts and establishing residency there. The rules were about the same for either state — although Massachusetts had had better divorce laws long before New York did, for instance — but Mother wanted privacy, so they chose to go away to do it. After their divorce, she would sometimes even tell people that her husband had died.

After the divorce, my father, Baker Brand, left the area, wandering to various places — Arizona, New Mexico, and California — usually working as a carpenter. We heard from him from time to time — a short letter or telegraph — but he didn’t write often and he sent little support. Meanwhile, of course, my mother stayed on the farm with us: Samuel, Leonard, Julia, and Effie. Samuel was about to marry Martha Hatch and move to Waseca, Minnesota.

❦   ❦   ❦

From the time I was very young, Mother had taught me how to sew and I had often made my own clothes as well as clothes for my mother, my brothers, and my sisters. In the early 1850’s a new type of sewing machine was invented by a man named Isaac Singer and began to be sold (though it was hard to find one in West Turin). But my mother was always interested in new ideas and when she realized what this machine could do, she became determined to get one, even trying to persuade her father to buy one for her. Singer also sold a treadle sewing machine, powered by a rocking foot motion. Mother thought these might work, but it was the one that came out in 1856 that she really wanted: Singer manufactured their first machine model designed specifically for home use, complete with a wooden table and cabinet.

At first, Mother thought it would be too expensive and we would never be able to afford it. But then Singer developed a payment plan system where buyers had to put only $5 down. My mother was so excited. She was convinced that we could all make money by using this machine, making and selling clothes. As the oldest daughter, I got to use it the most and I learned quickly.

I was a dressmaker, not a seamstress. Dressmakers made the entire dress — seamstresses just did repairs and piece work. I knew how to make a woman’s dress easily and quickly. I was 22, a talented dressmaker, and I had been earning my living since I had been 17. I thought my skills would be enough. I was sure that I could find a way to make enough money to help support Mother and the rest of the family.

A year after my parents’ divorce, I told my mother I was going to Kansas City to find my way in the world. Julia very much wanted to go with me, but she was only fourteen and both my mother and I thought she was a little too young to go with me. I wasn’t sure just how and when I would get settled, and I thought it best that I leave Julia behind until I was more settled. She wasn’t happy about that decision, but in the end she agreed. I headed for Kansas City and within a year, my little sister Julia met and married a man. Despite losing their baby, she remained married. I encouraged her to join me in Kansas City whenever she wanted, and she would eventually join me there.

item.title: Book 1: Sarah Etta
item.description:
Chapter 1: Aunt Clarinda

My mother and my Aunt Clarinda were both beautiful women: dark hair and eyes, clear complexions, and statuesque figures. I know that men’s heads turned when my mother walked down the street, and I don’t think it was much different for my aunt. My grandmother gave birth to ten children: seven boys and three girls. Mother and Aunt Clarinda were her 4th and 5th babies, but their baby sister, Kay, died when she was only two. So, I suppose it was inevitable that they would become best friends and enjoy doing many things together, especially since they were the only girls.

Aunt Clarinda and my mother were just three years apart in age, my aunt being born first in 1828, and my mother three years later in 1831. They did many things together: helping their mother with household chores, going to school, and even marrying at close to the same time, although it was my mother who married first, in October 1848, and my aunt just three months later, in January 1849.

A substantial New York farmhouse, from Lewis F. Allen’s Rural Architecture (1852). The Higby family might well have lived in a similar house.

After their marriage, my mother and father lived just across the road from her parents in West Turin, New York. My mother had been born there, and so had my grandfather. In fact, my great-grandparents had a great deal to do with the founding of the community and my grandfather maintained a high social status in the community because of his family’s history.

Unfortunately, Aunt Clarinda married a man who lived in Ava, New York, which was about 25 miles south of West Turin in a heavily forested area. There were trails through the forest, but getting back and forth between the two towns was at least an hour’s trip, depending on your mode of travel. My mother and aunt were both having a lot of babies, and to travel that distance they would need a horse and carriage, so they just didn’t get to see each other often, but they did write letters to each other and their younger brother, James, sometimes delivered their letters to them.


West Turin, where the Higbys lived, and Ava, where Aunt Clarinda went to live after her marriage

I was born in 1853 and from the time I was very young my mother would tell me about Aunt Clarinda often. There were occasional visits when my Uncle James would bring my aunt and their kids to West Turin to visit my grandparents. I remember her, though the memories are a little vague. However, my mother talked about her often and would frequently remind me what had happened to my aunt. When she visited, I always thought Aunt Clarinda seemed happy, but I was young and didn’t always understand what was happening. My mother was always willing to talk to me and explain things. As I grew older, we became more like sisters than mother and daughter. From a young age, I loved and adored my mother and would do anything for her. She adored her sister, so I did, too.

❧   ❧   ❧

Aunt Clarinda and Uncle James had several children, a new baby about every two years. Linda and Almeda were born before me, while Andrew, Benjamin, and Eugenia were born after. Mother told me Aunt Clarinda was small and childbirth was difficult. After five children, she didn’t want another pregnancy. While my aunt was having children, my mother was also busy giving birth to my brothers, Samuel, Lafayette, and Leonard, as well as me and a little girl Mother named Susan, who survived only about eight months. During the time that my aunt was having her difficulties, my mother did not give birth, and I suspect that is because of all the stress and concerns for her sister.

Aunt Clarinda’s unhappy marriage to Uncle James led her to leave the home a year before his death, taking her children and a few of her belongings to my grandparents’ house. My parents and I lived nearby, so I often saw them. Shortly after, Uncle James took back the children except for Benjy, who was still nursing. Unbeknownst to me, my aunt was already pregnant with Eugenia.

After her other children were taken away, Aunt Clarinda left my grandparents’ home and they didn’t know where she was or what she was doing. She spent time with a man who had worked on my uncle’s farm. My mother thought Aunt Clarinda believed that if she slept with another man, Uncle James would divorce her. (At that time, in New York State, the only allowable reason for divorce was adultery.) But that didn’t happen. Instead, Aunt Clarinda returned to living with Uncle James after Eugenia was born.

Mother told me that Uncle James threatened to leave and go west, expecting Aunt Clarinda and the children to join him. My grandfather had given Aunt Clarinda the house deed, and she thought she could keep it if Uncle James left. But she learned, to everyone’s regret, that once married, all property belonged to her husband. Uncle James had also sued my grandfather for some furniture he had removed from the house when he came to get my aunt and children.

❧   ❧   ❧

Aunt Clarinda, trapped in a loveless and abusive marriage with five babies and no income, felt desperate. On August 27, 1857, my aunt bought four pairs of men’s socks and three shillings’ worth of arsenic from a store in Western. She explained that she was buying it for a neighbour whose rats had bitten a child’s ear. The store clerk measured out three ounces for my aunt and labeled the package “poison.” When she got home, my aunt said, she mixed it with butter, spreading it on bread and leaving it on the kitchen bench. She thought the rats would find it, but in the morning, she realized her husband had eaten it. This was always my aunt’s story, but I think my mother knew that her sister had indeed tried to kill her husband.

The day after my aunt purchased the arsenic, Uncle James went to work in the fields with his work hand and returned home shortly after, complaining of feeling unwell. For the next three days, his condition worsened, and neighbours and the doctor visited frequently. Aunt Clarinda also displayed concern, giving him tea, which the lawyers suspected was laced with arsenic, though this was never proven.

Following my uncle’s death, the doctor immediately informed the police of his suspicions that my uncle had been murdered, which led quickly to my aunt’s arrest. She was put in jail, though she did get to keep Eugenia with her as she was still being nursed.


❧   ❧   ❧

My mother instilled in me the importance of independence, a challenging concept for women in the 19th century. Despite my young age when my aunt was imprisoned for murdering my uncle, I absorbed every detail of her story from her daily lectures. My mother meticulously kept a scrapbook of newspaper articles, carefully cutting and pasting them in chronological order to create a compelling narrative, though her side of the story was somewhat overlooked at the trial.

The courthouse in Rome, New York

My uncle passed away in August 1857, but my aunt’s trial was over a year later in November 1858. My family stayed in Rome during the trial, but my mother wouldn’t let me join them, so I stayed with relatives and friends in West Turin. Aunt Clarinda attended every hearing, and the newspaper reported she didn’t seem to have suffered from her imprisonment, but she had a persistent cough and cold while awaiting her trial and was also nursing Eugenia. My grandfather, mother, and three of my cousins (Aunt Clarinda’s children) attended most of the sessions. The court struggled to find a jury due to some reluctance from various people, especially because it was a death sentence case, so they enlisted some of the spectators. My mother said many people, mostly women, came to watch. Many villagers testified that Aunt Clarinda had threatened Uncle James, including my aunt Jane, married to one of my mother’s older brothers, Jared.

At the trial, all of them, from the judges to the lawyers to the jury, were men. By the time my aunt went to trial, she had already been convicted in the court of public opinion. My grandfather hired three lawyers to defend my aunt: Ward Hunt was the chief defense attorney. My mother wanted to see the lawyer reveal how badly Aunt Clarinda was treated by Uncle James, but that never came out in the court testimony.

The District Attorney called the case “a deliberate and purposeful act that stands out in criminal history.” He emphasized the aggravating crime of murder by poison, especially when the fatal drug is administered by a wife to a husband; the wife, the lawyer said, was supposed to give comfort.

Perhaps one of the most confusing parts of my aunt’s story is the deed to the house which my grandfather gave to them as a wedding present. Because my aunt’s name was on the deed, she thought that her husband could not sell it without her permission. But she was wrong: the property belonged solely to my uncle. That was the law in New York State in the 1850’s. As well, my uncle had sold the house to a neighbour (although the neighbour had not yet received the actual document) because he was determined to leave and “go west.” He expected my aunt and the children to go with him.

❧   ❧   ❧

One letter my mother sent shortly before my aunt killed my uncle became a problem. Authorities found the letter in my aunt’s possession after my uncle’s death and suspected my mother was involved in a plot to murder my uncle. The defence repeatedly denied my mother’s involvement and did not even want the letter submitted to the court, but the prosecution included the letter in the record.

Here is my mother’s letter to my aunt:

Dear Sister,

I take this opportunity to write a few words to you. We are all well now, although I have been very sick.

Clarinda, I want to say something to you about what you wrote. I have received both your letters without Baker [my father] seeing them. I was down in the village when I got them. I bought twenty-five cents’ worth of opium, but I could not get any arsenic.

And now, Clarinda, I think you had better trust in the Lord for help, for I should not like to do as you say about the contract. I know I should get found out, and then there would be a dreadful fuss. And, Clarinda, that would not make any difference, for he could get another, so Baker says. I asked him if Jim could, and he said he could, because he can prove that he had such a contract. And if he disposes of the place there will be some way provided for you. He cannot give a deed of the place to anyone without your name to it. And now you look out that you do not sign it, for if you do he will have you put right, sister.

Tell me how he treats you, and how he acts, and how he talks about us. And have you got my letter that I wrote, sister? I do not think you can get anyone to take away any of the things unless they are a —. And now I tell you not to take anything yourself to put an end to you, for that would be very bad.

Clarinda, now [we can] fetch you and the children. I can talk better than I can write, sister. I have some of your money, and whenever you want it we will get it for you. I lost some of my money out of my drawer, and I did not know how, but yours might go too.

Write as soon as you get this, and burn this.

Good-bye, Clarinda.

From Sarah Brand.

The testimony about my mother’s letter aimed to prove its authenticity and potential significance to the prosecution. The prosecution attempted to link my mother’s opium purchase to the package sent to my aunt, but the defence objected, and the court excluded that evidence. The coroner testified that during the inquest, he received a letter and a small package, and he gave the letter to the district attorney (this would be the letter mentioned above). The package contained small papers with substances resembling salts and opium. This testimony established the authenticity of my mother’s letter and the existence of the opium-like package, which the prosecution used to suggest that there was suspicious communication between my mother and my aunt.

What was never discussed, and which angered my mother, were the things in the letter which indicated perhaps other concerns: “Tell me how he treats you, and how he acts, and how he talks about us” shows that my mother was convinced that Uncle James was not easy to live with. Later, she says “And now I tell you not to take anything yourself to put an end to you, for that would be very bad.” My mother worried that her sister was suicidal.

So the prosecution wanted this letter in evidence, and there was much debate about it between the lawyers. Because there was no evidence to suggest that my mother had assisted my aunt, the court finally decided to ignore it; however, they still allowed it to be submitted as “evidence.” During the defense’s presentation, my aunt’s attorney asked the court to exclude the letter, arguing it was delivered unopened the Sunday before the death and couldn’t be linked to the alleged poisoning on the previous Thursday. In the end, my mother was exonerated by the court, but not necessarily by public opinion.

Other testimony mentioned the bitter conflict between my aunt and uncle over the children. While these witness accounts seemed accurate, they failed to capture the terrible trap my aunt felt: an unhappy marriage, a desire for divorce, and a desire to keep her children. She simply wanted to be left alone to raise her children; she wanted no more pregnancies.

After my aunt returned to my uncle, many people noticed her and testified about what they saw. Most of her neighbours certainly knew that she was unhappy. I think, by the time she murdered my uncle, she was no longer completely sane.

Much of the testimony at the trial was medical and technical. My uncle’s stomach was examined and large amounts of arsenic were found in it. At the trial, as well, the admissibility of Aunt Clarinda’s alleged confession was debated. She had admitted to the coroner when he came to get the body that she had given him arsenic. Her defence attorney argued that it was an illegal confession, given under much duress, and should be excluded, but the district attorney and two of the three judges felt the confession should be admitted, and so it was.

My mother and my grandparents testified at the trial, trying to prove that her separation from James was brief, that any earlier marital issues were resolved, and that she had a valid reason for obtaining poison. My mother testified that she had exchanged private letters with Aunt Clarinda before James’s death, sent her a child’s dress and opium for her baby, and explained that references in her letter concerned family matters, land, money, and Clarinda’s desire to stay nearby. She also admitted that she and her sister had discussed pregnancy, opium, and even arsenic in connection with preventing another pregnancy.

My grandfather, Abijah Higby, and my grandmother, Tryphena Higby, both testified that when Aunt Clarinda separated from Uncle James in 1856, she returned to live with them. They claimed she was only briefly in Forestport and later returned to James after their differences were resolved. Abijah said he knew of no further trouble after the reconciliation. My father, Baker Brand, supported this by saying her stay in Forestport was only about ten days, attempting to counter the claim that she had run off with another man for an extended period.

❧   ❧   ❧

After hearing the arguments from both sides of the case, the jury deliberated for about half an hour before returning to court late in the evening at nine o’clock. They found my aunt guilty but recommended life imprisonment. The sentence was suspended until the next court term.

Shortly after my aunt’s conviction there were those who felt that she had not received a fair trial. It had to do with the fact that there were three judges and one of them was not always present for jury selection. Based on that, they decided in April 1859 to give my aunt a new trial which finally occurred in October 1859. Aunt Clarinda pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the first degree and was sentenced to life in Sing Sing. She had previously pleaded not guilty but withdrew her plea and pleaded guilty a few days before the trial.

My mother’s chilling news that my Aunt Clarinda had been convicted of murder and sentenced to life in Sing Sing Prison for Women left an indelible mark on my mother and on me. Tragically, my aunt passed away sometime in 1860, probably in the second half of the year and less than a year after she entered the prison, succumbing to infections and possibly a broken heart due to the prison’s appalling conditions.

Sing Sing Prison for Women

Inmates faced poor food, inadequate housing, and disease-ridden facilities, all under harsh rules that damaged their mental health. By 1860, the prison’s expansion and overcrowding worsened, facilitating the spread of infectious disease. Dr. W.N. Belcher, the prison physician for Sing Sing, noted in his report that the prisoners were generally unwell, with major health problems like influenza outbreaks, severe colds, and a three-month-long dysentery epidemic during winter. The three most likely conditions that my aunt might have had are: dysentery, a contagious disease caused by contaminated food and water; influenza or respiratory illness which could progress to pneumonia; or, tuberculosis, which was endemic in most prisons and made worse by the overcrowding.

❧   ❧   ❧

My grandmother, Tryphena Higby, was deeply affected by my aunt’s difficulties and died six years later. My grandfather remarried but died in 1871, just 11 years after Aunt Clarinda. Clarinda’s children — Linda, Almeda, Andrew, Benjamin, and Eugenia — were cared for by my grandparents, who struggled to find a place for them in the world. The gossip in West Turin about my aunt and her children — and also about my mother and whether or not she was involved — was everywhere, making it hard for all of us, but particularly difficult for Aunt Clarinda’s children. Both boys left New York and married, having families. The three girls lived quietly and disappeared from view even within their family. In short, we heard little about what they were doing and how their lives were progressing.

We also don’t know where my aunt is buried. A prison cemetery for the homeless closed down, and bodies were moved. My grandparents knew Clarinda’s whereabouts but never told my mother. Years ago, I’d see my mother cry alone and ask her why. She’d say it hurt so much to not know where her sister was buried.

My aunt’s situation was told to me over and over by my mother. She urged me to find a way to be independent and to not, in any way, be beholden to a man. I learned that lesson well and it was directly responsible for the life I chose.

“If a storyteller thinks enough of storytelling to regard it as a calling, unlike a historian he cannot turn from the sufferings of his characters. A storyteller, unlike a historian, must follow compassion wherever it leads him. He must be able to accompany his characters, even into smoke and fire, and bear witness to what they thought and felt even when they themselves no longer knew.”

Norman Maclean, Young Men and Fire

♥   ♥   ♥

Union Cemetery, founded on November 9, 1857, is the oldest public cemetery in Kansas City, Missouri. In Section 56, lot 2, stand two monuments quite different in style and colour.

The Brand and Ham monuments, Union Cemetery

One stone is a large pink spire — at least ten feet tall — which seems to go on forever and is certainly taller than any other nearby monument. A mother and daughter are buried here together under one stone:

On one side:

Sarah E. Brand
Died January 27, 1890
Aged 36 yrs 9 mos 23 days
Jesus Lover of my Soul
Let me to thy bosom lie.

On the other side:

MOTHER

Sarah Ann Brand
Wife of
John Kell
Feb 5, 1831
Feb 29, 1904
Asleep in Jesus

Beside the mother-and-daughter Sarahs is another monument, a grey stone sarcophagus with large letters — HAM — on both sides. At one end, the inscription reads:

Julia H Brand Ham
Oct 20, 1862
Dec 6, 1927
Rest in Peace

Their deaths are separated by 37 years, but despite marriages or other relationships, they chose to lie here together. A mother and two of her daughters: Sarah Ann Brand, Sarah Etta Brand, and Julia Harriet Brand. Together for eternity, but they surely miss Clarinda.

Sisters is a true story of five women to whom my husband is related: Sarah Ann Higby Brand and her older sister, Clarinda Higby Yourdon; Sarah Etta Brand and Julia Brand, two daughters of Sarah Ann; and Grace Brand Herrick, the daughter of Sarah Etta Brand. It takes place in the 19th century in three places: the Tug Hill plateau of northern New York, the farmlands of Minnesota, and the bustling and busy metropolis of Kansas City, Missouri. Each woman contended with the rules and laws which attempted to control her behaviour. Some succeeded far beyond their expectations; others struggled to understand and survive and endure.

item.title: Family Legacies: Janie in Illinois
item.description:
Chapter 2 of Family Legacies by Susan Kay Overturf

Rural Illinois, August 1894

Little Janie Byrne McAlan led a quiet and sometimes lonely life. The only child of Martha Sarah Byrne and William Daniel McAlan, who had married in the late 1880s, Janie had been born seven days after her parents’ first wedding anniversary.

Janie’s father, William McAlan, was a successful auctioneer by the time he met and married Janie’s mother. William’s father had fought in an Illinois volunteer company at the siege of Vicksburg during the Civil War. Ill with tuberculosis, he had made his way home to his wife and five children before the war ended and, nine months later, his wife gave birth to William. William‘s mother died when he was only two, and he didn’t get along with his new stepmother. At fifteen, he left home to fend for himself and seemed to be a bit of a drifter, going from job to job.

The Byrne family weren’t too pleased with their daughter being courted by young William. James Byrne was proud of his Irish heritage and had worked hard to make a life for himself and his family in the United States. He had enlisted in a Delaware regiment where he was detailed to guard a powder plant. After the war, he had worked as a cooper but eventually he bought his own land to farm. He and his wife had seven children, including their oldest daughter, Martha, who was Janie’s mother. While Janie’s father had been lonely and unhappy as a child, her mother had enjoyed a warm and loving family.

The McAlan and Byrne families lived within a mile of each other in Logan County. When William came courting Martha, her parents disapproved, but they finally agreed to the marriage. As an auctioneer, William travelled a great deal and when Martha fell ill, her parents cared for her. Janie frequently found herself alone, conjuring up pretend games and creating imaginary playmates, unaware of the tensions among the adults in her life.

On this hot August day while the Cullens moved into their new home in Nebraska, Janie, her mother and grandmother returned from visiting neighbours. As they stepped on to the porch, Janie heard her mother — who looked quite pale — say to her grandmother: “I must lie down.”

Grandmother Byrne took Martha’s hand. “Lean on me, dear,” and she opened the screen door. After getting Martha inside, she looked back at her granddaughter. “You stay here, Janie, on the porch.”

Janie frowned.

She felt tears behind her eyes, but she did not want to complain. Instead she pleaded, “Please, Grandmother, can I look at the flowers?”

“All right,” Grandmother Byrne sighed, “but you go no further than that.”

Janie nodded. As soon as her grandmother disappeared, her attention went to the handsome bed of flowers. She ventured down the three wooden steps to the flowerbed. The flowers’ vibrant colors appealed to her; she wanted to touch each petal, but Grandmother had been always quite clear: “Remember, child, do not touch!” Janie knew it was unwise to disobey her grandmother, who could be equally stern or gentle, depending on whether or not someone had tampered with her flowers.

To Janie, the flowerbed was a feast of sight and smell: tall, white-and-yellow buttercups, white field daisies with golden centres, black-eyed Susans, purple coneflowers, and swamp candles. Spiked loosestrifes — the tallest and most prolific — ranged from rose to deep magenta. Janie understood why her grandmother always said that the flowers brought her happiness, because Janie also felt that they did the same for her.

“Hello, flowers,” she said, as she always did, “how are you today?”

Janie preferred not to choose a favorite amongst them. Some had turned to face the mid-afternoon sun but others still faced east. With the late-afternoon temperature at 102 degrees, they drooped in the heat. Janie picked up the watering can and slowly sprinkled the flowers, watching the drops catch the sunlight and sparkle, before coming to rest on the leaves and blossoms.

Janie’s mother had not been well for as long as Janie could remember.

The grown-ups sometimes talked about it in whispers, when they didn’t think she could hear, but she heard words like “lung disease” and “consumption,” even if she didn’t understand their meaning. She saw the paleness of her mother’s face and heard her cough in the night.

People often thought that Janie was only four years old, but she had had her fifth birthday ages ago, and still people thought she was four. Her mother or grandmother brushed out her long, dark-brown hair each night. As always, today she wore a pretty ribbon, yellow to match her dress, which pulled her hair behind her neck. Her brown eyes matched her hair. She often stood on tiptoes to reach things, but Grandmother Byrne told her, “When you are as tall as me, you’ll be tall enough.” Janie looked forward to school starting in September. Her mother had promised her that soon they would buy her school supplies and her mother would go with her on the first day.

Time passed and no one came.

Janie grew bored and warm in the sun, so she climbed up the three steps to the shady porch and listened at the door. She could hear nothing. Everyone must be upstairs, she thought.

She skipped over to the porch swing and crawled up into it. She moved it back and forth, almost lulled by the sound of its squeaking — back and forth, back and forth. She looked up and counted the ceiling boards. When she had reached the number twelve, Uncle Alex came out of the house, smiled at her but said not a word. He ran down the road towards Janie’s home. Janie watched him until he disappeared, his figure melting in the heat waves. Once he was gone, she went back to counting the boards in the ceiling, but soon she would lose track of where she was in her counting and have to start over again.

As she began to re-count for the tenth time, Uncle Alex returned with her father beside him.

Janie was puzzled. “Papa, what are you doing here?”

“Everything’s all right, Janie. Your Uncle Alex tells me that your mother’s weak. I thought I‘d come over and visit with her. You’re being a good girl, Janie, so you just stay here and wait for someone to come get you. I’ll see you soon.”

Janie’s father disappeared into the house with her Uncle Alex. A hint of worry crept into Janie’s thoughts. Why would Papa come over today? I wonder what’s happening. I hope Mama’s all right.

Now time began to drag.

Janie left the swing and walked back and forth across the front porch. At the far end, she climbed up on the railing and slipped onto the far side to get a better look at the clouds overhead. They were white and puffy and they didn’t look like rain clouds. As she stared at them, they took on different shapes: an elephant, a giraffe, and then a funny looking frog with too many legs. The animals changed as the clouds moved, but she grew bored with her private game. She climbed back over the railing into the shade of the porch and, as she walked across, she watched the cracks between the boards. “Step on a crack, you’ll break your mother’s back,“ she said out loud, so she walked the full distance of the porch without touching a single crack. She repeated her feat three more times.

The afternoon grew longer and longer. People came and went: her father, her four uncles, her Aunt Sarah, her grandfather, the doctor. But no one told her anything, and she began to get hungry. Just when Janie thought that she could not possibly manage another minute alone on the porch, her aunt came out.

“Aunt Sarah! I’m tired! I’m hot! What’s happening? Where is everyone? Is Mama all right?”

Sarah looked at her niece with soft eyes. "Janie, your mother’s had one of her long naps. She’s feeling better now, and she’d like you to come. You mustn’t stay for long and tire her, though."

Janie jumped off the swing and followed her aunt into the house, up the stairs to the first bedroom on the left. Something is very wrong, she thought. No one spoke, as she entered the room with her aunt. The closed curtains let in little light and precious little air. I can’t breathe, Janie thought. It took several minutes for her eyes to adjust to the darkened room.

She knew everyone, but no one looked at her. Her father, usually full of laughter, sat in a chair beside her mother’s bed, his gaze entirely on his wife’s face. On the high, four-poster bed lay her mother, dressed in a pretty white night dress with ruffles at her neck, her hair combed and pulled back behind her with a few curls escaping around her face. Janie could not see her mother‘s arms and hands, as they hid below the blankets, which seemed odd on so warm a day. Her skin looked white and her eyes were closed. Out of the corner of her eye, Janie could see the doctor who was mixing something from bottles in his medical bag. Two of her uncles stood at the foot of the bed, somber and still. Her grandmother stood at the head of the bed, just to the right of her mother’s shoulder. Her grandfather got up from a rocking chair near the window. He took Janie’s hand, but they did not move.

Janie wanted to run away, but just as she thought to make her feet move in the opposite direction, her mother’s eyes opened and her pale face turned towards her and smiled. “Janie.” Janie could barely hear her. “Come see your mama.” She took her arm out from under the blanket and extended it towards Janie.

Janie walked slowly towards her mother, one hand in her grandfather’s and the other hand in her aunt’s. Aunt Sarah picked her up and set her down on the edge of the bed, her feet dangling several inches above the floor. Her mother seemed peaceful and calm, but Janie felt awkward and afraid. Everyone stared. She knew something was wrong. Why doesn’t anyone look at me? she wondered. Why is everyone here?

Her mother took Janie’s hand in hers.

“Janie,” she repeated, but her voice was soft and she gasped for air. “I love you — more than anything else in the world. I’ll always love you. Even if you don’t see me — you must believe that. If I go away, will you be a good girl? Obey your father and your grandparents?”

Janie found it hard to swallow, let alone speak. What does she mean she is going away? Her eyes grew larger but she remained voiceless. The room frightened her — it was dark and sad. Finally, she managed a quiet “yes.”

Her mother closed her eyes and sighed deeply. She gently squeezed Janie’s hand, and then she said something strange and unforgettable. “Janie, your Aunt Sarah can be your mother. She’ll love you as though you were her own child. Will you let Aunt Sarah be your mother if I go away?”

What does that mean? I love Aunt Sarah, but she‘s not my mother. You‘re my mother. I love you. Janie looked at her mother’s sombre face. I must make this promise to make my mother happy, she thought. I must tell her this even if it’s a lie. She swallowed again — she was very thirsty. “Yes, Mama, I can do that.”

Janie’s mother nodded her head. “Good. That gives me peace. You must go now, Janie.”

Janie felt her grandfather’s big arms pick her up.

Janie began to cry and she reached over her grandfather’s shoulders for her mother. No, no, she thought. I don’t want to leave! I want to go back to Mama! I want to stay with her! Her grandfather saw her tears and heard her sobs, but he did not hear her thoughts.

The door closed. Janie kept her eyes glued to the bedroom door until it disappeared from her sight. Wordless, Grandfather carried her to the kitchen and placed her on a chair at the table. In front of her, he placed a small plate of food. “Eat,” he said. “You need to eat, child.”

Janie picked up some bread and nibbled at it. She thought of her mother upstairs. She felt tears rising in her eyes, and she couldn’t swallow her food.

“Eat,” her grandfather said again. “Finish your potato and your milk.”

Janie swallowed the food, but she tasted nothing. The tears formed again, but she knew that Grandfather Byrne would not want her to cry, so she squeezed her eyes shut and held back the tears. Just as she finished eating, Aunt Sarah came into the room. “I’ll be taking you home, Janie, so that you can go to bed.”

“Will Mama and Papa come with us?” When her aunt said nothing, she pleaded, “Why can’t I stay here?” Again, her aunt did not reply.

Aunt Sarah took her hand and together they walked down the road. Janie felt the heat coming up from the road. Even when her mother was sick, Janie usually spent the night under the same roof with her mother. Janie looked back at her grandparents’ house. I want to go back, she said to herself. She tugged at her aunt’s hand. “Aunt Sarah, I want to go back.”

“No, Janie, you can’t. Come along now.”

If I don’t go back to that room, Janie thought, I will never see my mother again. “Please, Aunt Sarah. Please.”

Aunt Sarah looked down at her young niece. “Janie, I know how you feel. I would like to go back, too. But we must leave your mother now and let her rest. God will decide what happens to her.” They walked on in silence.

Janie went to bed that night, alone in her parents’ house but for Aunt Sarah, and waited for the terrible news she knew would come. She did not sleep much. From her bed, she could see out the window but no breeze came with the hot air. Janie made a wish on one of the stars: "Please let Mama be all right." She thought that, if she could stay awake all night and keep wishing on stars, her mama would be fine in the morning. If she fell asleep, she feared what her Aunt Sarah would tell her.

When Janie awoke at dawn, she instantly remembered the events of the night before. She crept out of bed and found her aunt, who had fallen asleep in the rocking chair in the parlor, looking quite uncomfortably crumpled and stiff. Janie pulled on her hand and Aunt Sarah’s eyes opened.

“Aunt Sarah? Are you all right? Where are Mama and Papa?”

Sarah’s eyes softened. “Oh, Janie. Your Uncle Alex came just a little while ago.” Sarah stiffly sat up, reached over and pulled Janie into her lap. “Janie, your mama has gone to heaven. You will be able to talk to her whenever you want but you won’t see her. I promise you, she’ll hear you. I promise.”

Janie watched a tear trail down her aunt’s cheek, and she understood her aunt’s meaning, even though she suspected that her aunt thought she did not understand because she was only five. But Janie knew. Mama is dead — just like our old cat, Tuffy. When I found him, Mama helped me bury him and she told me that Tuffy was in heaven. Now Mama’s in heaven, just like Tuffy. She closed her eyes and squeezed them. Inside, she cried and cried and cried. Oh, she thought, I should have stayed awake! She felt her aunt’s arms around her but she wanted her mama’s arms. She would have given anything to take back the long night, even to go back to that room where her mama had been and to sit beside her forever and ever. She knew she would be lonely for the rest of her life, but she would try hard to always remember her mama. The love for her mother in her heart would never be shared until she met Simon Cullen.
